standards.title: Governance Standard No. (1): Shari’a Supervisory Board: Appointment, Composition and Report
standards.applicability: Applies to every Islamic financial institution (IFI), which must have a Shari’a supervisory board (para 3); the SSB's composition must exclude directors or significant shareholders of the IFI (para 7); no other exclusions stated in the document.
term_names: Statement of Sources and Uses of Zakah and Charity Funds
standards.structure: Introduction (para 1); Definition of Shari’a Supervisory Board (para 2); Appointment of Shari’a Supervisory Board and Fixing of Its Remuneration (paras 3-6); Composition, Selection and Dismissal of Shari’a Supervisory Board (paras 7-8); Basic Elements of the Shari’a Supervisory Board's Report (paras 9-24) — Title (para 10), Addressee (para 11), Opening/introductory paragraph (para 12), Management's responsibility (para 14), Scope paragraph (paras 13, 15-19), Opinion paragraph (paras 20-21), Date of report (paras 22-23), SSB's signature (para 24); Publication of the Report of the Shari’a Supervisory Board (para 25); Publication of Fatwas, Rulings and Guidelines of the Shari’a Supervisory Board (para 26); Effective Date (para 27); Adoption of the Standard (unnumbered, p.891); Appendix: Example Report of Shari’a Supervisory Board (unnumbered, pp.892-893).
key_points: SSB is defined as an independent body of specialised jurists in Fiqh Al-Mua’malat (Islamic commercial jurisprudence), entrusted with directing, reviewing and supervising IFI compliance with Shari’a Rules and Principles (para 2).
SSB may include a member who is not a Fiqh specialist but who is an expert in Islamic financial institutions with knowledge of Fiqh Al-Mua’malat (para 2).
Fatwas and rulings of the SSB are binding on the Islamic financial institution (para 2).
Every IFI shall have an SSB appointed by shareholders at the annual general meeting upon recommendation of the board of directors, taking local legislation and regulations into account (para 3).
Shareholders may authorise the board of directors to fix the SSB's remuneration (para 3).
Terms of engagement between the SSB and the IFI must be agreed and recorded in an appointment letter (para 4).
The IFI must document and confirm the SSB's acceptance of appointment; the appointment letter should generally reference the IFI's compliance with Shari’a Rules and Principles (para 5).
The SSB shall appoint a supervisor(s), from among its members or any other person, to help it perform its duties (para 6).

The SSB shall consist of at least three members; it may seek consultants with expertise in business, economics, law, accounting and/or others; it should not include directors or significant shareholders of the IFI (para 7).
Dismissal of an SSB member requires a recommendation by the board of directors and approval by shareholders in a general meeting (para 8).
The SSB's report must contain seven basic elements: title, addressee, opening/introductory paragraph, scope paragraph, opinion paragraph, date of report, and SSB signature (para 9).
The report should have an appropriate title and be addressed as required by the engagement's circumstances and local laws and regulations (paras 10-11).
The opening paragraph should identify the purpose of the engagement, with illustrative wording provided (para 12).
The scope paragraph should describe the nature of the work performed, including illustrative wording on reviewing the principles and contracts relating to transactions and applications (para 13).
The report should clearly state that IFI management is responsible for Shari’a compliance while the SSB forms an independent opinion based on its review (para 14).

The scope paragraph should confirm that appropriate tests, procedures and review work were performed, including examining, on a test basis of each type of transaction, evidence supporting Shari’a compliance (paras 15-16).

Where appropriate, the report should state that the financial statements were examined for the appropriateness of the Shari’a basis of allocating profit between equity holders and investment accountholders (para 17).
Where appropriate, the report should state that all earnings realized from sources or by means prohibited by Shari’a Rules and Principles have been disposed of to charitable causes (para 18).
Where the IFI prepares a Statement of Sources and Uses of Zakah and Charity Funds, the SSB's report should state whether the Zakah calculation complies with Shari’a Rules and Principles (para 19).

The opinion paragraph should state whether contracts, transactions and dealings comply with Shari’a Rules and Principles, covering the profit/loss allocation basis approved by the SSB and, where appropriate, charitable disposal of prohibited earnings and Zakah calculation compliance (para 20, items a-d).
If the SSB ascertains that management has violated Shari’a Rules and Principles or the SSB's fatwas, rulings and guidelines, the violations must be reported in the opinion paragraph (para 21).

The report must state the period covered and be dated as of the completion date of the review, and must not be dated earlier than the date the financial statements are signed or approved by management (paras 22-23).
The report must be signed by all members of the SSB (para 24).
The SSB's report shall be published in the IFI's annual report (para 25); publication of the fatwas, rulings and guidelines issued by the SSB during the year is recommended, not mandated (para 26).
The standard is effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 1999 A.D. (para 27).

standards.applicability: Applies to all IFIs, including Islamic finance windows, across all sectors; RSAs may apply it to other institutions in their jurisdictions as appropriate; also applied insofar as practicable by institutions other than IFIs adopting AAOIFI GSs, including social finance institutions (para 2). Also applies to the external stakeholders of the institutions (including RSAs) to the extent of their respective responsibilities as defined in the standard (para 3).
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR5); Introduction/Overview & Rationale(s) for issuing this standard (IN1-IN3); Objectives of the standard (para 1); Scope (paras 2-3); Definitions (para 4 a-n); Principles of Shari’ah governance — listed paras 5-18, elaborated paras 19-81: Principle 1 ‘Shari’ah governance framework’ (para 5; discussion paras 19-22); Principle 2 ‘Role of regulatory and supervisory authorities’ (para 6; paras 23-29); Principle 3 ‘Central Shari’ah board’ (para 7; para 30); Principle 4 ‘Unique organs of institutional Shari’ah governance framework’ (para 8; paras 31-34); Principle 5 ‘Role of those charged with governance and senior management’ (para 9; paras 35-51); Principle 6 ‘Shari’ah supervisory board’ (para 10; para 52); Principle 7 ‘Shari’ah compliance function’ (para 11; para 53); Principle 8 ‘Internal Shari’ah audit function’ (para 12; para 54); Principle 9 ‘External Shari’ah audit’ (para 13; paras 55-57); Principle 10 ‘Islamic finance windows’ (para 14; para 58); Principle 11 ‘Islamic finance subsidiaries / associates’ (para 15; para 59); Principle 12 ‘Considerations related to the business model and stakeholders’ interests’ (para 16; paras 60-65); Principle 13 ‘Applicability to different sectors’ (para 17; paras 66-75); Principle 14 ‘Transparency and disclosure’ (para 18; paras 76-81); Effective date (para 82); Appendix A Adoption of the standard; Appendix B Basis for conclusions (BC1-BC24); Appendix C Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H11).
key_points: Standard applies to all IFIs, including Islamic finance windows, across all sectors; RSAs may extend it to other institutions; applied insofar as practicable to non-IFI institutions adopting AAOIFI GSs, including social finance institutions (para 2).
Standard also applies to external stakeholders of the institutions, including RSAs, to the extent of their respective defined responsibilities (para 3).

Defines the hierarchy of ‘Shari’ah principles and rules’: (i) AAOIFI Shari’ah standards; (ii) regulator’s regulations entailing Shari’ah requirements; (iii) rulings of the central Shari’ah board of the jurisdiction (if any); (iv) applicable AAOIFI FASs insofar as Shari’ah related; (v) approvals/rulings of the institution’s SSB — SSB clarification prevails in case of ambiguity (para 4(l)).

Defines Shari’ah non-compliance risk as the risk from an IFI’s failure to comply with Shari’ah principles and rules, a sub-set of operational risk that may result in legal, financial or reputational risk (para 4(k)).

Defines Investment risk reserve (IRR) as amounts appropriated from profit/loss-taking investors’ income to cushion credit, market and equity investment risk of residual future losses after impairment (para 4(d)).

Defines Profit equalisation reserve (PER) as amounts appropriated to maintain a level of return for profit/loss-taking investors (and shareholders), managing rate-of-return risk including displaced commercial risk (para 4(i)).

Defines ‘public interest institutions’ to include listed institutions, institutions with publicly traded securities (e.g. Sukuk), and retail IFIs whose investment accountholders/depositors/unitholders/participants exceed 10,000 unless the RSA defines otherwise (para 4(h)).

Principle 1 requires each institution to have a comprehensive Shari’ah governance framework ensuring effective and independent oversight of Shari’ah compliance of products, services, processes and business operations (para 5).

Principle 4 sets the minimum organs of the Shari’ah governance framework: Shari’ah supervisory board (SSB), Shari’ah compliance function, internal Shari’ah audit function, and external Shari’ah audit (ESA) (para 8).

Principle 9 requires an annual external Shari’ah audit (ESA); mandatory for public interest institutions three years after the effective date, strongly recommended for all other institutions in the interim (paras 13, 55-56).

Principle 5 requires TCWG to approve Shari’ah-related governance policies, oversee CSB/SSB rulings implementation, oversee the internal control framework, oversee senior management performance against Shari’ah governance objectives, and promote a Shari’ah-compliant corporate culture (para 9; para 37 a-e).

TCWG must formally assess SSB performance at least annually, covering competence, knowledge and contribution of each member, but limited to administrative assessment only; senior management may never perform this assessment (para 44).

Principle 3 recommends (not mandatory) that RSAs/governments establish central Shari’ah boards (CSBs) to harmonise Islamic banking/finance practice in the jurisdiction (para 7); the board decided during drafting to keep this as ‘recommended’ rather than ‘strongly recommended’ (BC23).

Principle 12 requires institutions to apply proportionality based on relative size, business model, nature of operations, and the stage of development of the Islamic finance industry in the jurisdiction (paras 16, 62).

Principle 13 covers sector applicability: fully applicable to banking and Takaful sectors; applied with proportionality to Islamic capital markets (ICM), Islamic deposit insurance, Islamic microfinance and Islamic social finance institutions (paras 17, 66).

For Islamic Capital Market (ICM) products, the SSB must comprise three or more Shari’ah scholars or be sourced via an external Shari’ah consultancy firm; where a CSB exists, ICM products must comply with CSB requirements (para 70).
RSAs are expected to cooperate with other RSAs to manage cross-border ICM activities in light of differing Shari’ah interpretations or differing Shari’ah governance requirements (para 72(c)).

Principle 14 requires transparency and disclosure of Shari’ah governance to shareholders, customers, stakeholders and market participants, proportionate to size, complexity, structure, economic significance and risk profile (paras 18, 76-77).

Takaful institutions must disclose, for each fund: the adopted Shari’ah screening methodology, any purification payments made on non-fully-Shari’ah-compliant assets/businesses, and the amount of purification payments held but not yet paid (para 80 a-c).

Takaful institutions must disclose Qard Hasan policy (including impairment and waiver/write-off requirements), its movement (receipts, payments, impairment, adjustments), and future projections of the funds’ ability to repay the Qard Hasan (para 81 b-c).
Effective date: the standard is effective on or after 1 January 2026, with earlier application encouraged (para 82).

Standard issued as final on 28 Jumada II 1446H, corresponding to 29 December 2024, following AGEB’s 37th meeting (12-14 Dhul-Qa’dah 1445H / 20-22 May 2024) which unanimously finalised and approved it for issuance (Appendix A; H11).

History: AAOIFI and IFSB jointly developed an exposure draft ‘IFSB-AAOIFI Revised Shari’ah Governance Framework for Institutions Offering Islamic Financial Services’ issued 16 Ramadan 1444H / 7 April 2022; the two bodies subsequently agreed to separately review and issue guidance within their own respective mandates, and AGEB approved development of six standalone governance standards (including this one) covering matters not addressed elsewhere in existing AAOIFI governance standards (H1-H3).

The board decided the standard would be principle-based overall, but adopted a more prescriptive approach where a thin line exists between principle and rule, particularly on issues of Shari’ah compliance, fairness, justice or equity leaving little room for interpretation (BC2).
divergence_notes: “cooperate with other RSAs to manage cross-border activities in the ICM in the light of differing Shari’ah interpretations or differences in the relevant Shari’ah governance requirements” (para 72(c)).

During public consultation, “some stakeholders ... were of the view that the Shari’ah principles and rules hierarchy should not be defined at all to encourage Shari’ah scholars’ Ijtihad”, while others felt it should be left to each RSA to define for its own jurisdiction (BC6).

standards.title: Governance Standards No. (2): Shari’a Review
standards.applicability: Applies to Shari’a Supervisory Boards (SSB) of Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) performing Shari’a reviews to ensure compliance with Shari’a Rules and Principles as reflected in fatwas, rulings and guidelines (para 1); to be read in conjunction with ASIFI No. (1) para 7 and ASIFI No. (2) para 17, requiring coordination between SSB and external auditor (para 2); responsibility for actual Shari’a compliance rests with IFI management, not the SSB (para 5); no exclusions stated.
term_names: Governance Standard for Islamic Financial Institutions (GSIFI)
standards.structure: Introduction (paras 1-2); Definition and Principles of Shari’a Review (para 3); Objective of the Review (para 4); Responsibility for Compliance with the Shari’a (paras 5-6); Shari’a Review Procedures (paras 7-13), comprising Planning and designing Shari’a review procedures (paras 8-11), Executing Shari’a review procedures and preparation and review of working papers (para 12), and Documenting conclusions and report (para 13); Quality Assurance (paras 14-15); Report (para 16); Responsibility for Implementation of the Standard (para 17); Effective Date (para 18); Adoption of the Standard (unnumbered, p.903).
key_points: Purpose is to establish standards and guidance assisting SSBs of IFIs in performing Shari’a reviews to ensure compliance with Shari’a Rules and Principles as reflected in fatwas, rulings and guidelines (para 1).
Appointment, composition and report of the SSB is dealt with in AAOIFI Governance Standard No. (1): Shari’a Supervisory Board: Appointment, Composition and Report (para 1).
Where applicable, the fatwas, rulings and guidelines of a Higher Shari’a Supervisory Board also apply (fn 1).

Standard should be read with ASIFI No. (1): Objective and Principles of Auditing (particular reference to paragraph 7) and ASIFI No. (2): The Auditor’s Report (particular reference to paragraph 17), requiring close coordination between the SSB and the external auditor (para 2).

Shari’a review is defined as an examination of the extent of an IFI’s compliance, in all its activities, with the Shari’a, covering contracts, agreements, policies, products, transactions, memorandum and articles of association, financial statements, reports (especially internal audit and central bank inspection), circulars, etc. (para 3).
The SSB shall have complete and unhindered access to all records, transactions and information from all sources, including professional advisers and IFI employees (para 3).
Objective of the review is to ensure IFI activities do not contravene the Shari’a; achieving this requires that the Shari’a as defined in para 1 is mandatory (para 4).

SSB is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the extent of an IFI’s compliance with the Shari’a, but responsibility for the compliance itself rests with the management of the IFI, with consideration given to the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations (para 5).

SSB shall assist management by providing guidance, advice and training on Shari’a compliance; the Shari’a review does not relieve management of its responsibility for Shari’a-compliant transactions, and management must provide the SSB all Shari’a-compliance-related information (para 5).
An IFI shall not restrict the Shari’a review noted in paragraph 3; any restrictions imposed shall be included in the SSB’s review report to shareholders (para 6).
Shari’a review is carried out in three stages: planning review procedures; executing review procedures and preparing/reviewing working papers; and documenting conclusions and report (para 7).

Planning stage: procedures shall be planned for effective and efficient completion, requiring a complete understanding of the IFI’s operations (products, size of operation, locations, branches, subsidiaries and divisions) and obtaining a list of all fatwas, rulings and guidelines issued by the SSB (paras 8-9).

Plan shall be documented including sample selection criteria and sizes, taking into account complexity and frequency of transactions; review procedures are then designed to cover all activities, products and locations, ascertaining whether SSB-approved transactions/products were undertaken and related conditions met (paras 10-11).

Execution stage review procedures normally include: understanding management’s awareness, commitment and compliance control procedures; reviewing contracts/agreements; reascertaining transactions were for SSB-authorised products; reviewing other information/reports such as circulars, minutes, operating and financial reports, policies and procedures; consultation/coordination with advisors such as external auditors; and discussing findings with IFI management (para 12).
Execution of the review procedures shall be documented in work papers that are complete, neat and cross-referenced to review procedures (para 12).

SSB shall document its conclusions and prepare its report to shareholders based on work done and discussions held; the report shall be read at the IFI’s annual general meeting, and a detailed report, when warranted, shall also be issued to management (para 13).
SSB shall implement adequate quality control policies and procedures to ensure the review is conducted in accordance with this standard (para 14).

Quality control procedures may include review of all work papers to ensure review procedures were properly understood and executed, with additional discussions held with management if required to ensure significant matters were covered (para 15).
SSB report to shareholders of an IFI shall be based on GSIFI No. (1): Shari’a Supervisory Board: Appointment, Composition and Report (para 16).
Responsibility for implementation of this standard, and of GSIFI No. (1), lies with the management of an IFI (para 17).
Effective date: standard is effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1420 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D. (para 18).
Standard was adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in its meeting No. (15) held on 27-28 Safar 1419 A.H., corresponding to 21-22 June 1998 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).

standards.title: Governance Standard No. (4): Audit and Governance Committee for Islamic Financial Institutions
standards.effective_date: Financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H. or 1 January 2002 A.D. (para 15)
linked_standards: AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of Islamic Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) generally, defining the role, responsibilities and establishment requirements of an Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) for an IFI; no exclusions stated (para 1, para 10).
term_names: Governance Standard for Islamic Financial Institutions (GSIFI)
Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of Islamic Financial Institutions
standards.structure: Introduction (para 1); Importance of AGC (para 2); Functions of AGC (para 3); Responsibilities of AGC (paras 4-9) covering review of internal controls (para 4), review of accounting practices and audit plan (para 5), review of interim and annual accounts and financial reports (para 6), Ethics (para 7), reviewing compliance with Shari'a rules and principles (para 8), reviewing use of restricted investment accounts' funds (para 9); Establishing the AGC (paras 10-13) covering Constitution (para 11), Membership (para 12), AGC planning and meetings (para 13); Reporting (para 14); Effective Date (para 15); Adoption of the Standard; Appendix: Specimen Terms of Reference (Constitution, Membership, Attendance at Meetings, Frequency of Meetings, Authority, Responsibilities, Reporting Procedures).
key_points: Purpose of the GSIFI is to define the role and responsibilities of an Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) for an IFI, the requirements for establishing it, and the prerequisites for an effective AGC (para 1).

AGC importance derives from achieving IFI objectives through greater transparency and disclosure in financial reporting, and enhancing public confidence in the IFI's genuine application of Shari'a rules and principles (para 2).

AGC assists the board of directors through four functions: preserving integrity of the financial reporting process; safeguarding interests of shareholders, investors and other stakeholders; providing assurance on reliability of financial information; and acting as an independent link between management and stakeholders (para 3).
AGC's role on internal controls requires sufficient understanding of the IFI's business and control environment, with extensive interaction with management, internal and external auditors (para 4).

Internal control responsibilities (paras 4a-4j) include: comprehending major risks; monitoring management's control consciousness; reviewing pressures on management (e.g., remuneration, market expectations); monitoring management reporting adequacy; reviewing internal audit resources, scope and reporting lines; reviewing effectiveness of internal control systems; reviewing central bank and regulatory inspection findings; reviewing the IFI code of ethics; reviewing the IFI's Shari'a-compliance monitoring system; and ensuring related-party procedures are implemented (paras 4a-4j).

Review of accounting practices and audit plan responsibilities (paras 5a-5e): understanding high-risk/judgmental areas; reviewing accounting policies, new standards and reporting requirements; reviewing audit nature and scope; ensuring coordination and independence of internal/external auditors; and considering appointment, resignation or dismissal of SSB members, chief internal auditor and external auditors (paras 5a-5e).

AGC shall review interim and annual accounts and financial reports before submission to the board, to ensure their completeness, fairness and accuracy, and shall be briefed on interim reporting methodology (para 6).

Review of interim/annual accounts specific responsibilities (paras 6a-6f): ensuring compliance with Shari'a, legal and regulatory requirements; ensuring compliance with all AAOIFI standards; reviewing judgmental areas, accounting estimates and unusual transactions; reviewing significant audit adjustments; determining appropriateness of the going concern assumption; and presenting a balanced assessment of the company's position (paras 6a-6f).

Ethical principles governing the AGC, drawn from AAOIFI's Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of Islamic Financial Institutions (Sections 2 and 3): faith-driven conduct, professional competence and diligence, trustworthiness, religious legitimacy, objectivity, and professional conduct and technical standards (para 7, fn 1).
AGC must work to facilitate Shari'a reviews by the SSB and the internal audit function to ensure adherence to the fundamental ethical values (para 7).
AGC reviews reports produced by the internal Shari'a review and the SSB to ensure appropriate actions are taken, and may invite an SSB member to attend its meetings (para 8).

For Islamic banks, funds are mobilized from investors based on a Mudaraba contract or agency, covering both unrestricted and restricted investment accounts; restricted accounts are off-balance sheet, requiring management to invest per the agreement and allocate profits per agreed, Shari'a-compliant terms, with AGC coordination with internal Shari'a reviewers and external auditors for effective monitoring (para 9).
The specific structure of the AGC varies by IFI and country of establishment, though certain establishment features are common (para 10).

Constitution: the AGC shall be formally established by the board of directors from its non-executive members; the board appoints the AGC chairman; the AGC shall be vested with sufficient authority to act with independence and integrity (para 11a).

The Terms Of Reference (TOR) of the AGC shall be set out in writing, state its powers and responsibilities, and empower it to investigate matters within its jurisdiction; the TOR is used by the board, AGC members, management, outside legal counsel, SSB, internal Shari'a reviewers and external auditors (paras 11b-11c).

Membership attributes: AGC members shall be knowledgeable about the institution's business and applicable regulations/laws, understand related Shari'a rules and principles and their application to the IFI's products and services, and have sufficient knowledge of AAOIFI's standards (para 12a).

Term of office and size: the AGC's term of office matches that of the board of directors' members; the AGC shall not have less than three members, representing a balance of views and experience (para 12b).
Remuneration: AGC members' remuneration may be based on a board recommendation to the general assembly meeting, or on prevailing laws and regulations of the country (para 12c).
AGC planning and meetings: the AGC shall, with the consent of the board of directors, prepare internal by-laws governing AGC meetings and who may attend without voting rights (para 13).

Reporting: AGC reports are submitted to the board of directors through the board chairman, copied to the chief executive officer; AGC members' names may be mentioned in annual reports; the AGC chairman is recommended to report significant matters to the board chairman; the board discusses the AGC's work based on its quarterly report (para 14).
Effective Date: the Standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2002 A.D. (para 15).
Adoption: the Standard was adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in its meeting No. (21), held on 8 Safar 1422 A.H., corresponding to 2 May 2001 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).

Specimen TOR Appendix - Membership and Authority: the AGC shall not have less than three members, appointed by the board from non-executive members, with a quorum consisting of a majority; the chairman is appointed by the board; and the AGC is authorized by the board to investigate any activity within its TOR, seek information from any employee, and obtain outside legal or other independent professional advice and secure attendance of outside experts if necessary (Appendix - Membership, Authority).

Specimen TOR Appendix - Responsibilities include reviewing interim/annual financial statements focusing on accounting policy changes, major judgmental areas, significant accounting adjustments, the going concern assumption, compliance with AAOIFI accounting standards, compliance with regulatory/stock exchange/legal requirements, and compliance with related-party procedures (Appendix - Responsibilities, item c).

standards.title: Governance Standard No. (5): Independence of Shari’a Supervisory Board
standards.effective_date: financial periods beginning 1 Muharram, 1429 A.H., or 1 January 2008 A.D. (para. 14)
linked_standards: AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of IFIs
Code of Ethics for the Employees of IFIs
standards.applicability: Applies to members of Shari’a Supervisory Boards (SSBs) of Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) regarding independence, monitoring of independence, and resolution of independence issues (para. 1); responsibility for implementation of the standard lies with the management of an IFI (para. 13); no exclusions stated.
standards.structure: 1. Introduction (para 1); 2. Independence (para 2); 3. Importance of Independence of SSBs (paras 3-4); 4. Objectivity (paras 5-9); 5. Continuous Assessment (para 10); 6. Basis of SSB Independence (para 11); 7. Resolution of Issues of Independence Impairment (para 12); 8. Responsibility for Implementation of This Standard (para 13); 9. Effective Date (para 14); Adoption of the Standard (unnumbered, p.942); Appendix: Examples of Possible Issue of Independence Impairment (unnumbered, pp.943-944).
key_points: Standard's purpose is to provide guidance for SSB members of IFIs on independence, monitoring of such independence, and ways to resolve issues of independence (para 1).

Independence defined as an attitude of mind that does not allow the viewpoints and conclusions of its possessor to become reliant on or subordinate to influences and pressures of conflicting interests, achieved through organizational status and in an objective way (para 2).
The principle of objectivity imposes obligations on SSB members to be fair, intellectually honest, and free of conflicts of interest (neutral) (para 2).
Independence of SSB members enhances public confidence in the IFI's Shari'a compliance and helps achieve the IFI's fundamental objectives via SSB independence and objectivity (para 3).

SSB members bear responsibility to the public who rely on their services requiring independence, including clients, credit grantors, governments, employers, employees, investors, and others relying on SSB objectivity/integrity for Shari'a compliance (para 4).

Objectivity is an independent mental attitude SSB members must maintain when performing Shari'a supervision; SSB members must not subordinate their judgment on Shari'a supervision matters to that of others (para 5).
SSBs must perform Shari'a supervision with an honest belief in their work and must avoid potential and actual situations that impair their ability to make objective professional judgments (para 6).
SSB members must not be employees of the same IFI (para 7).
SSB and its members must not be involved in any manner with managerial decisions and operational responsibilities of the IFI (para 8).

Three-year preceding-period rule: where an SSB member is, or was within or immediately preceding an engagement period, an officer of a client or partner/employee of an IFI, the preceding period must be not less than three years (para 9).

SSB members must continuously assess their relationships with their IFIs to identify situations that may impair independence, and resolve or report to the SSB such situations where an issue of independence impairment is present or may reasonably be inferred (para 10).

SSB independence standards and rules are derived from Shari'a rules and principles, similar to the AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of IFIs and the Code of Ethics for the Employees of IFIs; this standard should be read jointly with those two codes (para 11).

Resolution of independence impairment follows four steps: (a) document the issue, (b) review the issue internally within the SSB, (c) if the issue persists after internal review, the affected SSB member must resign and the IFI's General Assembly must be notified, (d) local laws and regulations must be considered at all levels of conflict resolution (para 12).
Responsibility for implementation of this standard lies with the management of an IFI (para 13).
Effective date: this standard is effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram, 1429 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2008 A.D. (para 14).

Standard adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in its meeting No. (29), held on 29 Rabi' II and 1 Jumada I, 1426 A.H., corresponding to 7 and 8 June 2005 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).

Appendix example – financial involvement: financial involvement with, or in the affairs of, clients (direct or indirect, e.g. shares ownership, guarantees) affects independence and may lead a reasonable observer to conclude it has been impaired (Appendix).

Appendix example – personal and family relationships: relationships to a third degree of relationship with an SSB member can affect independence, particularly with a member of the Board of Directors, CEO, or other executive/management team member of the IFI (Appendix).

Appendix example – fees: recurring fees from an IFI or group of connected IFIs representing a large proportion of an SSB member's total gross fees, or a large proportion of unpaid fees for prior periods, may raise doubts about independence (Appendix).

Appendix example – contingency fees: Shari'a supervision services should not be offered or rendered under an arrangement where no fee is charged unless a specified finding or result is obtained, or where the fee is otherwise contingent on findings/results (Appendix).

Appendix example – performance-related bonus: Shari'a supervision services should not be offered or rendered under an arrangement where the SSB member benefits from a bonus payment related to the IFI's performance (Appendix).

Appendix example – goods and services: acceptance of goods, services, or undue hospitality from an IFI may threaten independence; only goods/services within the normal courtesies of social life are acceptable (Appendix).

Appendix example – actual or threatened litigation: litigation involving an SSB member and an IFI may cause concern that the normal relationship with the client is affected such that the SSB's independence and objectivity may be impaired (Appendix).

Appendix example – long association: continuation of the same SSB member on a Shari'a supervision engagement over a prolonged period may threaten independence; an IFI should ensure orderly rotation of SSB servicing on the engagement so that at least one SSB member is rotated every five years (Appendix).

standards.title: Governance Standard No. (6): Statement on Governance Principles for Islamic Financial Institutions
linked_standards: Shari'a Supervisory Board: Appointment, Composition and Report
Audit and Governance Committee for Islamic Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) as the minimum standard for establishment of governance structures, addressing those charged with governance, management, and other parties in a functional capacity relating to an IFI's business (paras 11-12); no exclusions stated.
standards.structure: 1. Introduction (paras 1-4); 2. Rationale for the Establishment of the Framework (paras 5-9); 3. Objectives of the Statement (paras 10-12); 4. Basis for Governance (paras 13-32), with 4/1 Enhancing confidence (paras 16-20), 4/2 Shari'a compliance (paras 21-22), 4/3 Business model (paras 23-24), 4/4 Stakeholders' interests (paras 25-28), 4/5 Social responsibility (paras 29-31), 4/6 Business ethics and culture (para 32); 5. Principles of Governance (paras 33-66), comprising all 12 principles: 5/1 Principle (1): Effective Shari'a compliance structures (paras 33-36); 5/2 Principle (2): Fair treatment of equityholders (paras 37-41); 5/3 Principle (3): Equitable treatment of fund providers and other significant stakeholders (paras 42-44); 5/4 Principle (4): Fit and proper conditions for board and management (paras 45-46); 5/5 Principle (5): Effective oversight (paras 47-52); 5/6 Principle (6): Audit and governance committee (paras 53-54); 5/7 Principle (7): Risk management (paras 55-59); 5/8 Principle (8): Avoidance of conflicts of interest (paras 60-62); 5/9 Principle (9): Appropriate compensation policy oversight (para 63); 5/10 Principle (10): Public disclosures (para 64); 5/11 Principle (11): Code of conduct and ethics (para 65); 5/12 Principle (12): Appropriate enforcement of governance principles and standards (para 66); 6. Governance Structures (paras 67-74), with 6/1 Those charged with governance (para 67), 6/2 Governance structures (paras 68-70), 6/3 Limitations (paras 71-74); Adoption of the Statement (unnumbered, p.960); Appendix (A): Brief History of the Preparation of the Standard (unnumbered, pp.961-962); Appendix (B): Basis for Development of the Statement (unnumbered, p.963); Appendix (C): Meeting Stakeholder Information Needs (unnumbered, pp.964-965).
key_points: IFI stakeholders are wider than in conventional businesses; the interests of Rab Al-Mal and other capital providers are exposed to prejudice if governance is focused solely on equityholder benefits (para 2).

Those charged with governance of IFIs are held to the highest fiduciary standards, accountable not only to the equityholders who appointed them but to all key stakeholders and the community the IFI serves (para 3).
The Statement represents the framework for governance in IFIs and forms part of AAOIFI's pronouncements (para 6).

Purpose of the Statement: lay down key governance principles and concepts, help stakeholders appreciate governance roles, establish the foundation for future governance/compliance standards, and provide inter-linkage between current and future standards (para 7).

The Statement is intended to serve as the minimum standard for establishment of governance structures in an IFI, and will provide the foundation for future AAOIFI governance standards on individual principles (para 12).

Governance of an IFI goes beyond conventional corporate governance because of social and religious connotations; an IFI exists due to its ability to conduct commercial activity in accordance with Shari'a (para 21).
An IFI must have mechanisms to comply with Shari'a in all its financial and other dealings (para 22).
The IFI business model is characterized by Shari'a-compliant contracts carrying unique risks that both the IFI and its clients must recognize (para 23).

Principle (1) - Effective Shari'a compliance structures: an IFI must establish an effective structure covering the roles of BOD, SSB, management and auditors in relation to Shari'a compliance (para 33); interaction between the SSB and management must be transparent (para 35); the BOD bears responsibility for overall Shari'a-compliant conduct, and the SSB reports on compliance based on its review (para 36).

Principle (2) - Fair treatment of equityholders: an IFI must provide equityholders voting rights, dialogue opportunity, ability to select BOD/SSB members, and fair disclosure of financial and banking practices (para 37); controlling equityholders must safeguard the interests of minority equityholders (para 41).

Principle (3) - Equitable treatment of fund providers and other significant stakeholders: an IFI must ensure equitable, unbiased treatment and provide adequate financial/non-financial information for their decisions (para 42); fund providers must receive timely information about major business changes with material consequences to their interests (para 44).

Principle (4) - Fit and proper conditions for board and management: an IFI must lay down criteria governing appointment of BOD, SSB and management members, with selection transparent and predefined (paras 45-46).

Principle (5) - Effective oversight: the BOD must play an effective role in leadership, direction and monitoring of policy implementation, setting the tone for risk, compliance and other control activities consistent with Shari'a (paras 47-48); a sound internal controls framework comprises an effective control environment, key risk assessment, control activities, timely information/communication processes, and an oversight/monitoring process (para 51).

Principle (6) - Audit and governance committee: an IFI must have an audit and governance committee with terms of reference covering financial reporting, internal controls, internal audit oversight, external audit oversight, and Shari'a compliance (para 53); the committee should comprise non-executive BOD members and maintain independence from executive authority as practicable (para 54).

Principle (7) - Risk management: the BOD must be actively involved in setting the risk appetite and ensure appropriate policies/systems for identification, measurement, analysis, reporting and mitigation of risks (para 55); the BOD must approve the risk strategy and set tolerance levels for risks the IFI assumes (para 57).

Principle (8) - Avoidance of conflicts of interest: an IFI must set governance structures ensuring BOD members, SSB members, management, staff and external parties (e.g. external auditors, rating agencies) avoid conflicts of interest (para 60); the IFI must identify all potential conflict situations and institute codes/policies to avoid them (para 61).

Principle (9) - Appropriate compensation policy oversight: an IFI must set governance structures for remuneration policies of BOD, SSB and management, developed on an independent and transparent basis (para 63).

Principle (10) - Public disclosures: an IFI must adopt high standards of reporting satisfying the information needs of owners, investment accountholders, other counterparties, regulatory, Zakah and other agencies, with accurate, adequate, timely and fair reporting of financial and non-financial performance (para 64).

Principle (11) - Code of conduct and ethics: an IFI must adopt Shari'a-consistent policies and procedures promoting a code of ethical and responsible behaviour by BOD members, SSB members, management and employees (para 65).
Principle (12) - Appropriate enforcement of governance principles and standards: an IFI must have a mechanism to ensure governance principles and standards are adhered to and monitored (para 66).

Governance structures comprise, among other elements: a structure for setting governance objectives and monitoring performance; mechanisms for efficient resource use and accountability; a system for direction/management commensurate with risks; and a system of checks and balances protecting stakeholder interests (para 70).

There is no one-size-fits-all governance structure; effectiveness depends on human integrity and thinking abilities, not merely on prescribing particular structures or complying with pre-established rules (paras 71-74).
The Statement was adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in its meeting No. (30), held on 19 Shawwal 1426 A.H., corresponding to 21 November 2005 A.D. (Adoption of the Statement).

Unrestricted investment accountholders' information needs additionally cover: legal implications of commingled funds and corresponding assets; status of their funds in the event of failure of the Mudarib; BOD/management measures ensuring their interests are safeguarded and free from bias; and appropriate risk management measures relating to the Mudarib's fiduciary obligations (Appendix C).

standards.title: Corporate Social Responsibility, Conduct and Disclosure for Islamic Financial Institutions
linked_standards: Statement of Financial Accounting No. 2: Concepts of Financial Accounting for Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Financial Accounting Standard No. 1: General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
Code of Ethics for the Employees of Islamic Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to all IFIs regardless of legal form, country of incorporation, or size; mandatory sections apply to all IFIs while recommended sections apply only to IFIs with the financial or other capacity to comply; if the standard's requirements contradict the IFI's charter or local laws/regulations, a disclosure must be made to that effect; Islamic Insurance companies may disregard provisions not applicable to their operations (paras 2-3); IFI is defined as any institution acting as a financial intermediary that strictly abides by the provisions of Shari'a, including but not limited to Islamic banks and Islamic Insurance companies (fn 1).
term_names: Governance Standard for Islamic Financial Institutions (GSIFI)
standards.structure: 1. Introduction (para 1); 2. Scope of the Standard (paras 2-3); 3. Definition of CSR for IFIs (paras 4-6); 4. Objectives of the Standard (paras 7-9); 5. Responsibilities Under This Standard (paras 10-33) — 5/1 Structure of corporate responsibility (para 10), 5/2 Mandatory conduct (paras 11-20): 5/2/1 Policy for screening clients (paras 11-13), 5/2/2 Policy for responsible dealing with clients (paras 14-15), 5/2/3 Policy for earnings and expenditure prohibited by Shari'a (paras 16-17), 5/2/4 Policy for employee welfare (paras 18-19), 5/2/5 Policy for Zakah (para 20); 5/3 Recommended conduct (paras 21-33): 5/3/1 Policy for Qard Hasan (paras 21-22), 5/3/2 Policy for reduction of adverse impact on the environment (paras 23-24), 5/3/3 Policy for social, development and environment based investment quotas (paras 25-29), 5/3/4 Policy for par excellence customer service (para 30), 5/3/5 Policy for micro and small business and social savings and investments (para 31), 5/3/6 Policy for charitable activities (para 32), 5/3/7 Policy for Waqf management (para 33); 6. Disclosure Requirements and Presentation Treatment Options (paras 34-52) — 6/1 Mandatory disclosure requirements (paras 34-42): 6/1/1 screening clients (para 36), 6/1/2 dealing with clients (para 37), 6/1/3 earnings/expenditure prohibited by Shari'a (paras 38-39), 6/1/4 employee welfare (paras 40-41), 6/1/5 Zakah (para 42); 6/2 Voluntary disclosure (paras 43-52): 6/2/1 social/development/environment investment quotas (para 45), 6/2/2 par excellence customer service (para 46), 6/2/3 micro/small business and social savings (para 47), 6/2/4 Qard Hasan (paras 48-49), 6/2/5 charitable activities (paras 50-51), 6/2/6 Waqf management (para 52); 7. Responsibility Under This Standard (paras 53-56) — 7/1 Compliance and attestation function (paras 53-55), 7/2 Implementation function (para 56); 8. Effective Date (para 57); plus unnumbered Appendices (A) Brief History, (B) Reasons for the Standard, (C) Basis for Conclusions, (D) Definitions, (E) Examples of Disclosure Format and Presentation.
key_points: CSR for IFIs is defined as all activities carried out by an IFI to fulfill its religious, economic, legal, ethical and discretionary responsibilities as financial intermediaries for individuals and institutions (para 4).

The standard defines five responsibility types: religious (obey Islamic law), economic (financial viability, profitability, efficiency), legal (obey country laws/regulations), ethical (societal/customary norms not codified in law), and discretionary (social role implementing Islamic ideals beyond the other four) (para 5).
The standard does not focus on economic or legal responsibilities of IFIs, as these are assumed to be addressed by other accounting/governance standards and by state law respectively (para 6).

The standard applies to all IFIs regardless of legal form, country of incorporation or size; mandatory sections apply to all IFIs, recommended sections apply only to IFIs with capacity to comply, and disclosure is required where the standard contradicts an IFI's charter or local law; Islamic Insurance companies may disregard inapplicable provisions (paras 2-3).

Objectives: prescribe uniform CSR conduct/compliance standards codifying existing principles (not creating new rules), and ensure CSR activities and compliance are communicated to stakeholders in a uniform, truthful, transparent and comprehensible manner (paras 7-9).
Mandatory: IFIs shall implement a CSR policy for screening prospective clients, including screening criteria and Shari'a Supervisory Board approval of those criteria (para 11).

Screening policy may address compliance of prospective clients' investments with Islamic law, anti-money-laundering screening processes, review of the client's CSR compliance, review of investment impact on economy/society/environment, and abrogation-of-terms provisions; policy disclosure must be made to prospective clients before contractual agreement if the terms form part of the contract (paras 12-13).

Mandatory: IFIs shall implement a CSR policy for responsible dealing with clients, covering avoidance of onerous terms, ethical marketing, obligations/rights of parties, responsible financing terms assessed against repayment ability, remedies for breach, late-payment-charge treatment (including allocation to revenue or charity) and deferral for insolvent clients; disclosure required prior to contract execution and forming part of contractual terms (paras 14-15).

Mandatory: IFIs shall implement a CSR policy for earnings and expenditure prohibited by Shari'a (impermissible/haram transactions), requiring documented due process (description, amounts, reasons, SSB verdict, disposal method, and search for halal alternatives) for each impermissible transaction, supplementing existing AAOIFI standards (paras 16-17).

Mandatory: IFIs shall implement a CSR policy for employee welfare covering equal opportunity, merit-based pay/promotion, incentive/training schemes, maternity leave and flexible hours, maximum work hours, anti-discrimination measures and complaint avenues, affirmative-action quotas, elimination of child labour, elimination of rank-based class/race barriers, code-of-ethics-aligned conduct, and occupational health and safety; disclosure required to employees before employment commencement, preferably in the employee's native language (paras 18-19).
Mandatory: Zakah policy terms and conditions are governed by Shari'a Standard No. 35, Statement of Financial Accounting No. 2 section 4/6, and Financial Accounting Standard No. 9 on Zakah (para 20).

Recommended conduct comprises seven optional policy areas an IFI 'may' implement: Qard Hasan (para 21), reduction of adverse environmental impact (para 23), social/development/environmental investment quotas (para 25), par excellence customer service (para 30), micro and small business and social savings/investments (para 31), charitable activities (para 32), and Waqf management (para 33).

Qard Hasan policy may cover fund establishment, sources of funding, allowable beneficiaries, distribution circumstances, enforcement measures, write-off conditions for insolvent debtors, and strategies/quotas to grow charitable Qard Hasan lending; may be monitored yearly and supplements Statement of Financial Accounting No. 2 section 4/7 (paras 21-22).

Environmental policy may cover efficient/minimal use of non-renewable resources, employee education, alternatives to non-renewable energy/materials, and recycling initiatives; reviewable on a yearly basis (paras 23-24).

Social/development/environmental investment quota policies may set targets for poverty relief, orphans, indebted individuals, health services, research/education, SME development, cultural development, and discouraging social ills (social); growth potential, infrastructure, SME reliance, and alleviation of social/economic disadvantage (development); and environmental protection, reduced development impact, and renewable energy use (environmental); monitored yearly with revisions based on performance (paras 25-29).
Mandatory disclosure: a CSR report within the annual report must disclose the IFI's material mandatory-conduct policies, designed to be understandable to the general public (paras 34-35).

Mandatory disclosure requirements are specified for: screening-clients policy (para 36); dealing-with-clients policy (para 37); earnings/expenditure prohibited by Shari'a, supplementing Financial Accounting Standard No. 1 section 3/6 (paras 38-39); employee welfare policy including affirmative-action quotas/achievements (paras 40-41); and Zakah, per Financial Accounting Standard No. 1 and Financial Accounting Standard No. 9 (para 42).

Voluntary disclosure may be made in the annual report for recommended-conduct policies: investment quotas (para 45); customer service (para 46); micro/small business and social savings (para 47); Qard Hasan, supplementing Statement of Financial Accounting No. 2 section 4/7 and Financial Accounting Standard No. 1 section 4/7 (paras 48-49); charitable activities, supplementing Statement of Financial Accounting No. 2 section 4/6 and Financial Accounting Standard No. 9 (paras 50-51); and Waqf management (para 52).

The IFI's board of directors is responsible for ensuring compliance with the standard and must ensure an independent compliance audit is performed prior to attestation of CSR conduct; the compliance function tests both mandatory conduct and any recommended conduct the IFI has adopted, in form and substance (paras 53-54).

Board attestation comprises a signing declaration stating that management has proactively engaged in the mandatory and voluntary CSR provisions and/or that the annual report's CSR representations fairly reflect actual conduct (para 55).
Responsibility for implementing the standard lies with IFI management (para 56).
Effective date: the standard applies to financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1431 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 2010 A.D. (para 57).

standards.title: Governance Standard for Islamic Financial Institutions No. 8 Central Shari'ah Board
linked_standards: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 29 "Stipulation and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework"
GSIFI 1 "Shari'ah Supervisory Board: Appointment, Composition and Report"
standards.applicability: Applies to governance for Central Shari'ah Boards (CSBs) or similar bodies that oversee and advise regulators and government authorities on Shari'ah matters (para 3); does not apply to Shari'ah supervisory boards (SSBs) or other institution-level boards/committees, which are covered by separate standards (para 4, citing GSIFI 1 and 4).
standards.structure: Preface (paras PR1-PR7); Introduction - Overview and Rationale (paras IN1-IN3); Objective of the standard (paras 1-2); Scope of the standard (paras 3-4); Definitions (para 5); Appointment, composition and dismissal - First appointment, Subsequent appointments, Nomination committee, Remuneration, Terms of reference, Tenure (paras 6-15); Composition and selection - Composition, Diversity (paras 16-24); Removal and termination (para 25); Functions of the CSB - Fatwas, Advisory, Regulations, Oversight and limited supervision (paras 26-33); Other key functional provisions - Decisions, Secretariat, Self-evaluation and reporting, Confidentiality (paras 34-44); Responsibilities of the appointing authority / regulator (para 45); Fit and proper criteria - Shari'ah scholar members, Expert members (paras 46-50); Independence - Considerations for selection and appointment, Considerations for functioning (paras 51-54); Effective date (para 55); Transitional provision (para 56); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard (Members of the Board, Reservation, Working group and team); Appendix B: Basis of Conclusion (paras BC1-BC16); Appendix C: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (paras H1-H9).
key_points: CSB defined as a broad level board of specialized jurists in Fiqh al-Muamalat and experts (banking, finance, economics, law, accounting, etc.) providing guidance and advice on Shari'ah matters with limited supervision, established at country/jurisdiction level, with two basic types: a national Shari'ah board and a regulatory Shari'ah board (para 5b).

SSB defined as an independent body of specialized jurists in Fiqh al-Muamalat, which may also include expert member(s); the SSB directs, reviews and supervises IFI activities, and its Fatwas and rulings are binding on the IFI (para 5c).
This standard encourages, but does not mandate, the formation of CSBs, to achieve greater harmony in Islamic banking and finance practices within a jurisdiction (paras 1-2, PR7).

Two main models are currently prevalent: centralized (CSB alongside SSBs at institution level) and non-centralized (individual institution's Shari'ah board); AAOIFI does not intend to give preference to one model over the other (para PR5).
Within the centralized model, two categories exist: countries following a single central body and countries following multiple central bodies (para PR5).

Standard applies to governance for CSBs or similar bodies advising regulators/government authorities on Shari'ah matters; does not apply to institution-level SSBs and other institution-level boards/committees, covered by separate standards (paras 3-4).

Recommended minimum total board membership: 5 members for a board catering to a single industry segment (e.g. banking or insurance); 7 members for a board catering to multiple industry segments (para 18).
Majority of CSB members shall be Shari'ah scholar members selected from recognized Shari'ah scholars within or outside the country, meeting the fit and proper criteria for scholars (para 19).
Chairman and vice chairman(s) shall be elected from amongst the Shari'ah scholar members, by themselves (para 20).
Recommended term of the board is between 3 to 5 years, with a rotation policy addressing independence, continuity, self-evaluation, and a suitable cooling-off period for re-appointment (paras 14-15).

Quorum for any decision requires a majority of Shari'ah scholars present consistent with their proportion in the board's composition; for a Shari'ah ruling, the view of the majority of Shari'ah scholar members shall prevail (para 22).

Fit and proper criteria for Shari'ah scholar members includes: well-versed in Fiqh and Usul al Fiqh; suitable academic qualification; suitable practical experience preferably 10 but not less than 5 years in Fiqh al-Muamalat; good command of Arabic and business language(s); independence and freedom from conflict of interest, among other parameters (para 49).

Fit and proper criteria for expert members includes: basic understanding of Shari'ah principles, high standing in their field, suitable academic/professional qualification, demonstrable commitment, and independence/freedom from conflict of interest (para 50).
Functions of the CSB divided into three broad categories: advisory and Fatwa; regulations; and oversight and limited supervision (para 28).

CSB functions relating to advisory and Fatwa are mostly passive (reactive), provided only when asked by the appointing authority/regulator; the board becomes proactive only when it concludes major Shari'ah non-compliance has occurred, is perceived as known/approved by the board, and inaction would compromise stakeholders' interest (para 31).

Fatwas function includes issuing Fatwas/decisions, approving Sukuk structures and documentation for sovereign/government Sukuk as referred by the appointing authority, and validating IFI product structures as referred by the regulator (para 29).

Decisions of the board are taken by majority of votes at a duly constituted meeting with requisite quorum, with dissenting opinions documented and attached to majority decisions; decisions relating to advisory and Fatwa, with basis of conclusion, shall be compiled and published regularly subject to applicable law/regulations/regulator policy (paras 34, 36-37).

The board shall conduct self-evaluation exercises not later than annually, and shall prepare and submit an annual performance report, along with self-evaluation, to the appointing authority/regulator (paras 41-42).
Board and members shall maintain confidentiality of information and documents at all times, except information already public or requisitioned by a court or regulatory proceeding (para 44).

On first-time formation, Shari'ah scholar members shall not include more than one-third who work as Shari'ah advisors/board members for, or are significant shareholders of, a supervised IFI; on subsequent formation, no such member shall be included (para 51c).

On first-time formation, expert members shall not include more than one-third with significant financial dependence on the appointing authority/regulator or a supervised IFI; on subsequent formation, no such member shall be included (para 51d).

Remuneration of all members shall be equal (subject to additional pay for extra functions e.g. chairman/vice-chairman, secretarial or research duties on a time-based formula) and shall be disclosed to the public (paras 10-11).

Grounds for removal/termination of a board member, after adequate opportunity to be heard: proven professional misconduct or breach of a principal term of reference; or failure to attend the minimum number of meetings during the year without legitimate reason (para 25).

Standard effective from 1 January 2018; the transitional provision applies requirements on terms of reference, appointment, and constitution/reconstitution of CSBs to any such event occurring on or after the effective date (paras 55-56).
divergence_notes: Previously, differing evaluations by individual-institution SSBs gave rise to "conflicting rulings and eventually conflicting practices and products" that confused clients and investors (para PR3).
The board agreed that the existence of a CSB "does not preclude the diversity of opinions" among individual-institution SSBs, which continue to retain supervisory functions (BC5).
Diversity considerations for CSB composition include "representation from different schools of thought in the country / jurisdiction" (para 24b).

Voting rights are divided by matter type: for Shari'ah rulings, voting is reserved to scholar members only, reflecting a distinction in whose view governs Shari'ah matters versus other matters (BC9, para 22).

key_points: Shari’ah compliance is defined as the mechanism of ensuring the IFI's financial arrangements, contracts and transactions comply with Shari’ah principles and rules (para 3h).

Shari’ah principles and rules hierarchy: AAOIFI Shari’ah standards; the jurisdiction regulator's Shari’ah regulations; rulings of the Central Shari’ah Board (if any); AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards' Shari’ah-related requirements; and approvals/rulings of the IFI's SSB (para 3l, i-v).

Shari’ah non-compliance risk is defined as the risk arising from an IFI's failure to comply with Shari’ah principles and rules, a sub-set of operational risk that may result in legal, financial or reputational risk (para 3k).

Management of an IFI shall ensure a robust and effective Shari’ah compliance function exists and remains in operation (para 5); those charged with governance shall ensure management discharges this responsibility (para 6).

Preventive vs detective controls: the Shari’ah compliance function is a preventive control concerned with ex-ante work (para 13); internal/external Shari’ah review and audit are detective controls concerned with ex-post work (para 14).

The COSO integrated framework's five pillars structure the recommended Shari’ah compliance control environment: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring (para 22, fn 4).

IFIs shall adopt objective, risk-based monitoring of material Shari’ah non-compliance risk, documented by the risk management department in coordination with SCD and treated as a significant sub-set of operational risk for internal and regulatory risk reporting, including regulatory capital computation (para 25).

Hiring: management shall ensure personnel are suitable for their roles, with SCD consultation where necessary, and it is recommended personnel have understanding of and belief in Islamic finance products/services (para 30).

Training: basic Shari’ah training for all staff and in-depth training for specific functions, with continuous professional development coordinated with SCD (para 31); annual orientation/training for those charged with governance and senior management (para 32).

Technology: IFIs are encouraged to automate transactions for Shari’ah compliance (para 35); SCD shall coordinate system-based checks and flags with the IT team to provide preventive controls and alerts (para 36).
SCD shall be led by a senior, experienced Shari’ah compliance professional supported by an adequately qualified and experienced staff team (para 39).
Appointment of the head of SCD is the responsibility of management, subject to the concurrence of the SSB applying the specimen fit and proper criteria in Appendix B (para 40).
SCD is principally part of management: it reports to, is accountable to, and is evaluated/appraised for performance by senior management in consultation with the SSB (para 41).

SCD's primary functions (para 42, a-m) include: reviewing new-product policies/procedures; routine pre-execution transaction review; supporting the SSB; reviewing marketing documentation/communication; conducting structured ongoing compliance reviews; liaising with internal and external Shari’ah audit; assisting training; research for the SSB; facilitating pre-approvals and deviation approvals; and monitoring/enforcement of audit and review reports.

Dotted-line reporting: notwithstanding para 41, SCD shall establish a dotted-line reporting relationship with the SSB; where resources are inadequate, SCD shall also assume the SSB secretariat function (para 49).

Organizational independence: SCD is part of management but shall remain independent from managerial decision making, finance-related functions, legal, marketing and sales, and product development, except for providing reviews and inputs (para 51, a-e).

Secretariat of the SSB: where resources are constrained, SCD may perform the SSB secretariat function, subject to not creating self-review threats; in that case the head of SCD may also absorb the role of secretary to the SSB (paras 52-53).

Fit and proper criteria for head of Shari’ah compliance (Appendix B, a-d): well-versed in Islamic banking/finance and Fiqh al-Muamalat; a relevant university degree or equivalent qualification; preferably 10 years' (in no case less than 5 years, e.g. new markets, if allowed by the SSB) work experience in Shari’ah compliance/advisory/audit or related areas; and SSB approval of knowledge and skills.

SCD compliance report: periodic quarterly and annual reports to senior management and the SSB covering activities, risks and issues identified, and their mitigation/resolution (para 67); suggested annual report contents span scope, responsibilities, activities, key risks and mitigating controls, key issues and resolutions, prior-period follow-ups, and recommendations for improvement (para 68, a-h).
Effective date: the standard is effective on IFIs from 01 July 2021, with earlier application encouraged (para 71).

Basis of Conclusion (BC4): the board decided SCD's main reporting line is to management, with dotted-line reporting to the SSB, since SCD is principally part of management and accountable to senior management.

Basis of Conclusion (BC12): the board concluded there should be no outsourcing of the SCD as it is a unique management function; if needed, the function may instead be allocated to different organs/departments within the IFI in line with the standard's requirements.

Basis of Conclusion (BC10): the board voted a minimum of 5 years' experience for head of SCD in new markets, preferably 10 years, and directed that appointment of the head of SCD be subject to SSB approval per Appendix B.

The standard was approved by the AAOIFI Governance and Ethics Board at meeting No. 8, held 24-25 Shawwal 1439H corresponding to 8-9 July 2018 (Appendix A), and issued on 28 Safar 1440H corresponding to 6 November 2018 (Appendix D, H9).

standards.applicability: Applies to rating agencies conducting Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary rating engagements of Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs), with assessments performed at the institutional level (paras 2-4); IFIs are encouraged, not mandated, to have ratings conducted once in three years, preferably annually, and to publicly announce the results (para 5); the standard is a non-mandatory good-practice initiative unless a jurisdiction's regulator separately adopts it as mandatory (para BC32).
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR2); Introduction: Overview (IN1-IN3), Rationale (IN4); Objectives of the standard (para 1); Scope of the standard (paras 2-3); Responsibility (paras 4-5); Definitions (para 6); Appendix D: Basis of conclusions (BC1-BC32); Appendix E: Brief history of preparation of the standard (H1-H8).
key_points: Standard sets out principle-based guidance for rating agencies performing Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary ratings of IFIs on responsibility, acceptance, process, reporting and quality assurance; agencies remain free to develop their own detailed methodologies and rating scales (para IN1).

Elements of a Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary rating include: compliance with Shari’ah principles and rules, Shari’ah governance, related corporate governance, transparency and disclosure, ethics and values, and fiduciary performance (para IN2; para 6f).
IFIs are encouraged to have Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary ratings conducted once in three years, and preferably on an annual basis, and to publicly announce the results (para 5).
Assessments under this standard are performed at the institutional level; a second planned standard will cover publicly/secondary-market traded Islamic finance instruments (para 3, fn 1).

Definitions: “Rating agency” is a company/firm assigning Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary ratings; “Rating committee” is formed per paras 40-42; “Rating scale” is the final summarized output (alpha-numeric, other symbol, or less commonly a numeric score); “Rating service” is the accepted engagement to determine such a rating (para 6).

A rating agency eligible under the standard must be either a duly licensed credit rating agency with developed capacity/methodology, or a dedicated Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary rating agency with due involvement of credit-rating-experienced experts (para 8).

Rating agency must comply with AAOIFI's relevant code of ethics – pending a comprehensive AAOIFI code, presently the “Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of Islamic Financial Institutions” applies (para 10, fn 2).

Quality control must follow relevant professional requirements, particularly IOSCO's Statement of Principles Regarding the Activities of Credit Rating Agencies dated 25 September 2003, and must involve Shari’ah scholar(s) with expert knowledge of the benchmarked parameters (para 11, fn 3).

Rating agency shall not accept an engagement unless it is independent of the IFI, has performed a self-assessment of capacity, and has developed and publicized a consistent rating methodology (para 14).
Where independence threats or conflicts of interest exist, a rating agency may accept the engagement only after eliminating them, allowing a cooling-off period of 12 months (para 16).

Benchmarked parameters for Shari’ah compliance follow a stated hierarchy: AAOIFI Shari’ah standards; then jurisdiction regulator's Shari’ah regulations; then Central Shari’ah Board rulings (if any); then AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards' Shari’ah-related requirements; then the IFI's own Shari’ah Supervisory Board approvals/rulings (para 20).

Suggested weightage table for benchmarked parameters: Shari’ah compliance 30%-35%; Shari’ah governance framework 15%-20%; corporate governance practices related to Shari’ah governance 10%-15%; transparency and disclosure 10%-15%; ethics and values 10%-15%; fiduciary responsibility and performance 15%-20% (para 30).

Although the weightings of categories are independent of each other, a failure in a significant category, e.g. compliance with Shari’ah rules and principles, is treated as an overall failure (para 30, fn 5).
A rating scale is suggested to have a span of 5-10 stepped grades, each explained with expectations of the state of Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary responsibility associated with it (para 35).

Suggested rating scale (score ranges, %): iAAA 90+ (excellent level of compliance); iAA 80-89 (very good); iA 70-79 (good); iBB 60-69 (highly satisfactory); iB 50-59 (reasonable); iC below 50 (unsatisfactory) (para 36).

Rating committee shall comprise generally of five members, but in no case less than three members; not less than 33% of committee members must be independent of the rating agency (para 41; Appendix C, para 1).

All rating committee members must be given the opportunity to be heard; decisions are taken by majority; dissents are noted for record; on Shari’ah compliance matters, the majority view of the Shari’ah experts within the committee prevails (para 52; Appendix C, paras 8-9).
Rating agency must issue a Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary rating report with three components: rating score, full version report (to IFI management), and public report/press release (para 61).

Documentation of the rating engagement must be sufficient (quantitatively) and appropriate (qualitatively); minutes of rating committee meetings must be maintained and made part of the rating service documentation (paras 56, 58).
This standard is effective for Shari’ah compliance and fiduciary ratings issued on or after 01 July 2021 (para 63).

Standard was approved unanimously by the AAOIFI Governance and Ethics Board at its 11th meeting, 26-27 Sha'ban 1440H corresponding to 1-2 May 2019 in Bahrain, and issued on 5 Jumada I 1441H, corresponding to 31 December 2019 (Appendix A; Appendix E, H8).

Appendix C requires a minimum of 24 hours' notice to issuers before rating assignments and changes, to allow provision of new material information; a cooling-off period of a minimum of 12 months is required to eliminate existing conflict-of-interest situations (Appendix C, paras 20-21).

Board declined a stakeholder proposal to raise the rating committee's minimum independent-member threshold from 33% to 50%, reasoning the rating agency itself bears the risk/accountability while the committee's role is process improvement and quality assurance (para BC19).

Board concluded the standard should be issued as a non-mandatory, “good practice initiative,” though regulators in individual jurisdictions may, considering their market maturity and needs, adopt it as mandatory (para BC32).
