key_points: Standard is a revised and improved version of, and supersedes, GS 3 "Internal Shari'ah Review" adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board on 28-29 Safar 1420H, corresponding to 13-14 June 1999 (PR1).
Objective is to define and recommend a comprehensive framework for the internal Shari'ah audit (ISA) function of IFIs as part of their governance structure (para 1).

Internal Shari'ah auditors may refer to the International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF) in addition to this standard, unless contrary to or inconsistent with a requirement of this standard or Shari'ah (para 2).

Scope: standard provides broad guidelines and standardized practices for establishing/operating an ISA function providing internal assurance on the IFI's adherence to Shari'ah principles and rules to those charged with governance and the SSB (para 3).

Shari'ah non-compliance risk is defined as the risk arising from an IFI's failure to comply with Shari'ah principles and rules, a sub-set of operational risk that may result in legal, financial or reputational risks (para 4j).

Shari'ah principles and rules hierarchy comprises: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah standards; (ii) the respective jurisdiction's regulator's regulations entailing Shari'ah requirements; (iii) rulings of the central Shari'ah board of the jurisdiction (if one exists); (iv) AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards (FAS) insofar as Shari'ah-related; and (v) the IFI's own SSB approvals and rulings (para 4k, i-v).

Internal Shari'ah audit assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of controls pertaining to Shari'ah adherence, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function is an ongoing process of monitoring the bank's overall Shari'ah compliance environment (para 5; see also GS 9 paras 13-14, fn5).
An IFI shall not assert compliance with this standard unless it has complied with all the requirements of this standard (para 6).

Internal Shari'ah auditors shall comply with AAOIFI's "Code of Ethics for Accountants and Auditors of Islamic Financial Institutions" and the IIA's "Code of Ethics" and any other relevant code (para 7).

ISA function must fulfill the requirements of the IIA's Quality Assurance and Improvement Program (QAIP), including active involvement of Shari'ah expert(s) throughout the process, and must have a documented independent/peer review mechanism covering frequency, scope, and reviewer qualification (paras 8-11).

ISA function shall be independent of management (though not necessarily of the IFI itself), with unrestricted access to documents/reports/systems and direct communication with management, SSB and external Shari'ah auditors; auditors shall not undertake operational activities, product development, or Shari'ah compliance functions (paras 13-14, 16).

Primary objective of ISA is to provide an assurance opinion to those charged with governance and the SSB on the IFI's adherence to Shari'ah principles and rules, plus opinions on: adequacy of governance structure; adequacy of internal controls; and adequacy of risk assessment/management mechanisms for Shari'ah compliance (paras 17-18 a-c).

The audit committee shall ensure a robust and effective ISA function exists and remains in operation, keeping oversight; the SSB provides necessary input to the ISA function on a need basis (para 19).

Three possible forms for establishing the ISA function: (a) a separate department (the default for all IFIs); (b) a unit of the internal audit function, only if 4 conditions are met (small IFI/new market, adequate internal-audit capability, head meets fit and proper criteria, operational efficiency gained); or (c) outsourcing to a professional firm (paras 20-22 a-d).

ISA function may be outsourced to a professional firm only if the firm has adequate capability and meets fit and proper criteria per Appendix B, and the person assigned as head of ISA meets fit and proper criteria and is not involved in ISA assignments of more than three IFIs (multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs count as a single IFI for this purpose) (para 23 a-b).

Reporting line: primary reporting to those charged with governance (the audit committee), with dotted-line reporting to the SSB, since all Shari'ah issues must be dealt with by the SSB; draft reports and observations are shared with the SSB for its views/conclusions (paras 24-25).

Head of ISA fit and proper criteria (Appendix B.1): relevant university degree/professional qualification; well-versed in Islamic banking/finance and the Shari'ah principles hierarchy of para 4(k), with understanding of Fiqh al-Muamalat; preferably not less than 10-year work experience in Shari'ah compliance/advisory/audit or related areas (relaxable by the regulator in newer markets, fn6); SSB approval of knowledge/skills; necessary regulatory approvals (Appendix B.1 a-e).

Professional Shari'ah audit firm fit and proper criteria (Appendix B.2): necessary regulatory approvals; SSB approval of knowledge/skills and suitability; adequate qualitative and quantitative resources for each outsourced assignment; compliance with applicable professional standards, quality assurance processes and codes of ethics including independence/confidentiality (Appendix B.2 a-d).

Engagement (audit entity) process comprises 12 steps: planning; risk assessment; materiality assessment; sampling; internal Shari'ah controls assessment; controls testing (TOCs); evaluation of observations and Shari'ah non-compliances; assessment of residual risk; detailed procedures; closing meeting; reporting of audit observation (draft report); and issuance of final reports and audit ratings (para 44, process-flow chart).

Final reports due: periodic reports within a reasonable time but not later than 3 months from the end of the respective period; engagement (audit entity) reports within a reasonable time but not later than 1 month from completion of the engagement (if desired by the SSB and audit committee); SSB provides final comments on the draft periodic report within one month (paras 55-56).

Periodic reporting shall occur at least on a periodic (quarterly, half-yearly or at least annual) basis and shall include, as basic elements: title, addressees, overall ISA scope, opinion on overall adherence, summary of completed engagements/ratings, key risk matters, and status against the periodic plan (paras 57, 59 a-g).

An engagement (audit entity) report shall be issued for each individual audit engagement, including title, addressees, scope/description of the audit entity and period covered, opinion and rating for the entity, and a summary of key observations with follow-up items from prior periods (paras 60-61).

This standard is effective for internal Shari'ah auditors' reports covering periods beginning on or after 01 July 2021; transitional provisions apply the fit and proper criteria to new appointments/outsourcing engagements occurring on or after the effective date (paras 65-66).
This standard supersedes the earlier GS 3 "Internal Shari'ah Review" (para 67).
divergence_notes: There was considerable debate about whether the ISA reporting line should be to the SSB, but the board decided the primary reporting line should be to the audit committee (to maintain independence, given ISA's primarily audit-related mandate), with only a dotted-line to the SSB (BC8).

The minimum work-experience requirement for the head of ISA was debated extensively across working group, board, Shari'ah committee and public hearing sessions; the exposure draft proposed (preferably) 5 years given resource constraints in newer markets, but the board ultimately increased this to (preferably) 10 years, while allowing the respective regulator to permit relaxation in newer markets (BC21, fn6).

key_points: Sukuk (plural of Sak) are certificates of equal value representing undivided shares in ownership of tangible assets, usufruct and services, or assets of a particular project/investment activity, effective after receipt of value, closing of subscription and employment of funds (para 7.o).

Standard governs the entire lifecycle of Sukuk issuances - issuance, investment, maturity/termination, restructuring/rescheduling - and applies equally to instruments similar to Sukuk irrespective of nomenclature (para 3).
Implementation responsibility rests with those charged with governance and management of the originator (para 4).
Regulators shall consider developing an oversight mechanism for application of the standard alongside their own regulations (para 5).
In a Sukuk program comprising multiple issuances or tranches, each issuance or tranche shall independently fulfill the standard's requirements (para 6).
Five key pillars of Sukuk governance: Shari'ah compliance, accountability, fairness, transparency and responsibility; pillars (b)-(e) coincide with OECD principles (para 8).

Eleven governance principles (Pr.1-Pr.11) set out in a table covering Shari'ah compliance structures, fair/equitable treatment of stakeholders, effective oversight, audits and internal controls, risk management, avoidance of conflicts of interest, compensation policy oversight, public disclosures, code of conduct, and enforcement (para 9).

Seven organs of governance identified for a normal Sukuk issuance: those charged with governance, management, the SSSB, the trustee, internal audit function, external auditor, and external Shari'ah auditor (para 10).

Originator shall appoint a dedicated Sukuk's Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSSB) for every Sukuk issuance; an existing SSB meeting the standard's requirements may additionally serve as SSSB with necessary regulatory approvals (para 19).

SSSB composition, terms of reference and independence shall follow GS 1 and GS 2 requirements (with flexibility on member number/eligibility permitted under regulatory requirements) and independence per GS 5 and AAOIFI's code of ethics (paras 22-25).

Fatwa process requires two stages: a Provisional Fatwa on the proposed structure during planning/documentation, and a Final Fatwa after review of the final structure and documentation, per AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 29 (paras 27, 31, 34).
The Fatwa document shall be made public as a mandatory part of the prospectus, with a copy available to stakeholders throughout the Sukuk's lifecycle (para 29).

SPV requirements: absolute transfer of Sukuk assets creating a legal impediment for the originator/its creditors; no effective control or equity stake by the originator; no recourse to the originator absent an SSSB-approved Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement arrangement; SPV formation and documentation approved by SSSB (para 36, items a-e).

Sukuk assets shall be transferred to the SPV at a fair market value or a value reasonably close thereto; transfers at an inappropriate or exploitative value are prohibited for either party (para 46.d).
SSSB shall issue periodic reports on the overall state of Shari'ah compliance at a reasonable frequency, but at least on an annual basis (para 57).

SSSB report shall be addressed to those charged with governance and made available to Sukuk-holders, owners of the originator, those charged with governance, regulators and the central Shari'ah board as applicable (paras 59-60).

Both external Shari'ah audit of the Sukuk issuance (scoped per AAOIFI Auditing Standard (AS) 6) and external audit of financial reporting to Sukuk-holders are required at a suitable frequency but in no case less than annually (paras 83, 85, 95).

Financial reporting by the originator shall follow AAOIFI FAS 29 'Sukuk in the books of the originator'; financial reporting to Sukuk-holders shall follow FAS 34 'Financial reporting to the Sukuk-holders'; accounting policies subject to SSSB approval (paras 90-93).

Prospectus shall include at least 14 listed items for Sukuk-holder protection: originator/trustee/SPV details, independence controls, governance/SSSB member profiles, feasibility study, Sukuk asset description and valuation, profit distribution/loss sharing mechanisms, risks and hedging, participant details, legal framework and arbitration, credit enhancement recourse, tradability conditions, conversion/redemption options, final settlement mechanism, and termination/restructuring/default scenarios (para 79, items a-n).

Prospectus shall separately include Shari'ah-compliance-specific disclosures: SSSB member qualifications/powers, underlying contract structure and rules, SSSB confirmation of Sukuk-holders' ownership on execution of contracts, the detailed Fatwa as an integral legal document, escalation procedures, and disclosure of risk that courts may not accept Shari'ah principles for contractual interpretation plus remedial options (para 80, items a-f).

Termination of Sukuk permitted via mutual agreement, originator's unilateral early redemption (e.g. call options), trustee/Sukuk-holders' unilateral termination (including for default or potential default), or regulator-ordered early termination; must not result in unjustifiable material loss to Sukuk-holders (paras 67-68).

Restructuring or rescheduling of Sukuk arises from originator default/potential default, or from acquisition/merger/corporate restructuring of the originator, and requires thorough review and approval by the SSSB, Sukuk-holder representatives and the regulator (paras 69, 72).
Standard is effective on Sukuk issuances for financial periods beginning on or after 01 July 2021, with earlier application encouraged (para 102).

Transitional provisions on initial implementation: originators may elect not to apply the standard to already-completed lifecycle phases of a Sukuk (provided this does not cause non-compliance with another provision), or where the remaining time to maturity is less than 24 months from the effective date (para 103, items a-b).

key_points: Beneficiary (Mawquf Alaih) is defined as a natural/juristic person or a socially beneficial cause specified by the Waqif, eligible for the benefit arising from use/yield of Waqf assets per the Waqf deed (para 4a).

Nazir (or Mutawalli) is defined as an individual, board of Nazirs, juristic person or government agency responsible for managing and governing the Waqf and distributing its benefits per the Waqf deed (para 4e).

Ghallah (yield), per FAS 37, represents the net surplus from financial activities and other gains/losses attributable (adjusted for non-cash items and non-distributable items) to the beneficiaries (fn 2).

Standard applies to all types of Waqf and Waqf-based institutions regardless of legal structure; family Waqf are encouraged but not mandated to adopt it, since they are excluded from SS 60, without legitimizing violation of Shari'ah inheritance rules (para 2, fn 1).
Standard applies to a temporary Waqf created for a reasonably long period, generally no less than 5 years; shorter-duration temporary Waqf are also encouraged to adopt it (para 3).

Conceptually, upon creating a Waqf the Waqif loses ownership of it and the ability to transfer that ownership; according to a number of scholars ownership belongs to Allah Almighty alone and is not transferred to the Waqif's heirs, beneficiaries, the Nazir or the state (PP3).

Every Waqf must have a Nazir (unless the Waqif retains governance/management himself in rare circumstances); permitted forms are a board of Nazirs (strongly recommended), an individual Nazir, a juristic person Nazir, or a state Nazir (para 21).

An individual Nazir appointed by the Waqif is, as preferred governance practice, expected to nominate a board of Nazirs (with reasonable representation of independent members) within three years of his appointment (para 23).
The Nazir is the highest governance authority of the Waqf, holding responsibility both legally and per Shari'ah principles and rules, in whom all authority and powers are vested (para 24).

The Nazir must establish and implement a control framework in line with global good practice (e.g. COSO's Internal Control - Integrated Framework), scaled to the Waqf's nature and relative size (para 37).
Waqf assets shall in no case be subjected to a pledge or a charge created for the benefit of any party, including the Nazir or the Waqif (para 49).

Exception: Waqf assets may be pledged/charged to obtain Shari'ah-compliant financing only if subject to a well-documented risk policy approved by the Nazir and approved by the Waqf's Shari'ah supervisory board (para 50).

Nazir remuneration must be specified by the Waqif; if the Waqif is silent, a competent authority determines it, otherwise the Nazir is entitled to no more than fair remuneration per comparable fair market practice (para 51).

The audit committee must be independent of the Waqf and its management, with the majority (including the chairman) independent of the Nazir where the Nazir is not a board, established per AAOIFI GS 4 (paras 52-53).
The Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB) may comprise one or more members, preferably three or more, depending on the Waqf's relative size and operations (para 56).
The SSB's terms of reference follow AAOIFI GS 1 and GS 2, and its independence/ethics follow AAOIFI GS 5 and AAOIFI's Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals (paras 58-59).
The SSB must issue an annual report stating its opinion on the Waqf's compliance status with Shari'ah principles and rules (para 60).

The internal audit function reports functionally to the audit committee (or the Nazir if there is no committee) and administratively to senior management, following the IIA's International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing (paras 65-66).

The internal audit function must include an internal Shari'ah audit function relevant to the Waqf's operations, with guidance from AAOIFI's relevant standard on internal Shari'ah audit, GS 11 (para 71, fn 7).

The annual report must include, at minimum, the audited financial statements, a Nazir's report (financial and social performance, activities, investment risks, donations/grants), and an SSB report on Shari'ah compliance (para 79).

Financial reporting principles follow a hierarchy: (a) AAOIFI's financial accounting standard on Waqf (FAS 37), (b) other applicable AAOIFI FASs, then (c) jurisdictional GAAP insofar as it does not contravene Shari'ah principles and rules (para 80).

The external auditor performs the audit in accordance with AAOIFI Auditing Standards (ASs), supplemented by International Standards on Auditing for matters not specifically addressed by AAOIFI ASs (para 87).

The external auditor must additionally opine on whether the Waqf's revenue, expenditure and operations complied with the Waqf's objectives and Shari'ah principles, and whether Waqf assets were adequately safeguarded (para 88).
The standard is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021, with earlier application encouraged (para 91).
divergence_notes: On ownership of Waqf assets: "According to a number of scholars, the ownership of a Waqf belongs to Allah Almighty, alone" (PP3).
Terminology for the Waqf trustee was long debated between "Nazir" and "trustee"; "Mutawalli" is noted as an alternative term used in different jurisdictions and literatures (BC11-BC12).

standards.applicability: Applies to Waqf governance across all Nazir structures: board of Nazirs (paras 17-54, 70-72), individual Nazir (paras 73-74), juristic person Nazir (paras 75-76), and state Nazir (paras 77-78); to be read in conjunction with and in the context of GS 13, whose requirements prevail over this guidance note in case of any inconsistency (paras 1-2, 100).
standards.structure: Introduction (paras 1-2); Part A: What is Waqf? — Charity, private and joint Waqf (paras 3-7), Juristic personality of a Waqf (paras 8-9), Nature of Waqf assets and their selection criteria (paras 10-13), Fulfillment of the conditions of a Waqf (paras 14-16); Part B: The board of Nazirs — Mechanism for selection of members (paras 17-20), Suggested criteria for selection of members (para 21), Nomination of chairman and deputy chairman and their functions (paras 22-23), Functions of the deputy chairman of the board (para 24), Responsibilities of members of the board (para 25), Termination of membership of the board (paras 26-28), Removal of the Nazir (paras 29-31), Replacement and succession policy of members of the board (para 32), Continuing professional education of the board members (para 33), Meetings of the board (paras 34-39), general committee rules (paras 40-44), Nomination and remuneration committee (para 45), Investment and risk management committee (paras 46-47), Executive committee (paras 48-50), Governance committee (paras 51-52), Periodic evaluation of the performance of the board, its committees and members (paras 53-54); Part C: Pertinent policies and procedures for governance and internal control — Policy for stakeholders' relationship (paras 55-57), Conflict of interest policy (paras 58-59), Whistle-blowing policy (para 60), Document archiving policy (para 61), Complaints policy (para 62), External communication policy (para 63), Information security policy (paras 64-65), Human resource policy (paras 66-67), Code of professional conduct (paras 68-69); Part D: Specific provisions for different types of Nazirs — The board of Nazirs (paras 70-72), Individual Nazir (paras 73-74), Juristic person Nazir (paras 75-76), State Nazir (paras 77-78).
key_points: Waqf is defined as making a property or source of wealth inalienable and donating its usufruct to beneficiaries (para 3).
Waqf is classified as charitable (general public benefit), private (close group), or joint (both public and private beneficiaries) (para 4).
A family Waqf must adhere to inheritance principles and must not specify conditions contrary to Shari'ah (para 6).
From a Shari'ah perspective, a Waqf should have an independent juristic personality and a separate financial edict from the Waqif, beneficiaries and Nazir (para 8).
Waqf assets should be sustainable/long-term, owned by the Waqif at the time of creation, chosen at the Waqif's absolute discretion, and must be Shari'ah-compliant (paras 10-13).

Waqf deed conditions govern the Nazir's conduct; ambiguities are resolved via the Waqif's intention and customary practice, and deviation is only permitted where imperative and never contrary to Shari'ah or law (paras 14-16).

The Waqif appoints board of Nazirs members or sets eligibility/dismissal criteria; absent that authority, the board fills vacancies by resolution based on nomination and remuneration committee recommendation (paras 17-20).

Suggested selection criteria for board members include Shari'ah/legal capacity, piety and integrity, management experience, and absence of bankruptcy, crime or misconduct findings (para 21, sub-points a-l).

Unless the Waqif nominates a chairman, the board elects its own chairman and deputy chairman via a pre-approved election process; chairman duties include convening meetings and supervising agendas (paras 22-23).
The deputy chairman assists the chairman and assumes the chairman's duties during absence, illness, or membership termination until a replacement is appointed (para 24).

Board members' responsibilities include annual reporting to the regulator, Waqif and beneficiaries on developments and financial statements, meeting attendance, confidentiality, and avoiding conflicts of interest (para 25, sub-points a-n).

Board membership may terminate by death, end of term, approved resignation, loss of eligibility, dismissal by Waqif or court, or a serious breach decided by a court/competent authority or a two-third majority board vote (para 26).

The Waqif or competent authority may suspend or remove the Nazir for negligence, insolvency, incapacitating illness, or violation of law/Waqf deed, giving the Nazir an opportunity to be heard first (paras 29-30).
The maximum term for a member of the board of Nazirs is five years, unless otherwise prescribed by law (para 32).
The board of Nazirs of a typical Waqf should preferably meet at least 3 times a year, with meeting materials ideally circulated 2-3 weeks in advance (paras 35-36).

A quorum requires attendance of more than half the board members, in person or by visual communication with full voting rights, provided the member hears proceedings clearly and stays until the end (para 37).
The board may establish committees, preferably with no fewer than three and no more than five members; the majority of committee members and the committee chairman must be independent (paras 40, 43).

The nomination and remuneration committee's functions include proposing board/senior-management selection mechanisms, reviewing board structure, and proposing remuneration within the percentage allocated from the Waqf yield (Ghallah) per the deed or custom (para 45).

The investment and risk management committee manages Waqf assets with the objective of capital preservation while emphasizing yield (Ghallah) generation, and recommends investment strategy aligned with the Waqf deed (paras 46-47).
An executive committee, if established, must have at least three members, of whom at least one third are board members and two thirds are senior management (para 48).
The governance committee consists of three or more members, including at least one independent member who serves as its chairman (para 51).
A board of Nazirs typically consists of not less than three and not more than nine members, with a reasonable number independent of the Waqf, Waqif and other Nazirs (para 72).

The complaints policy should comply with ISO standard No. 10002:2014 (or equivalent) and recommends appointing a compliance officer even where not required by the regulator (para 62); the information security policy should consider ISO standard No. 27001:2013 (or equivalent) (paras 64-65).
A code of professional conduct for the board and management should principally align with AAOIFI's Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals (para 68).

key_points: Islamic crowdfunding (ICF) is defined as the type of crowdfunding that adheres to Shari'ah principles and rules in all its financial arrangements, contracts and transactions (para 7i).

Fund providers include investors, donors, creditors and Qard providers who provide funds through the crowdfunding platform, including those seeking returns and those seeking impact investment/social objectives (para 7g).

Commercial Islamic crowdfunding carries a promised return to fund providers, while Social Islamic crowdfunding is non-commercial and either impact-investment (no return, or return used for the intended purpose) or donation-based with no repayment intended (paras 7b, 7z).

Ongoing ICF issuance is a structure that is, by its nature, an ongoing transaction or venture, such as an Ijarah transaction or a Musharaka or Mudaraba venture, and may or may not have a fixed maturity date (para 7n).
Open-ended ICF issuance has no ceiling limit or specific period for investing and may or may not have an early redemption option (para 7o).

The standard enumerates 16 core principles of governance for Islamic crowdfunding, spanning Shari'ah compliance, stakeholder confidence, fairness, responsibility assignment, transparency, accountability, social responsibility, ethics, competence, supervision, risk management, disclosure, external Shari'ah audit, dispute resolution, internal control and enforcement (paras 11a-11p).
The operator is treated as an Islamic financial institution (IFI) and is therefore subject to the requirements of the relevant AAOIFI Governance Standards in addition to this standard (para 16).
The operator must establish a Shari'ah compliance function, including a Shari'ah compliance department (SCD), which coordinates with internal audit and IS/IT audit functions (paras 17, 20).

A trustee, independent of the operator and issuer, must hold raised funds in trust accounts and release them to the issuer only once the targeted amount is achieved, there is no material adverse change during the offer period, and any regulator-required cooling-off period has expired (paras 24-27).

The Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB) must be appointed by the issuer in consultation with the operator for every ICF issuance, though a shared operator-wide SSB or an outsourced advisory firm nominating at least three eligible members is permitted (paras 45-46).

The SSB's Fatwa must be documented with reasoning, made public as part of the prospectus, and cover the issuance structure, contracts, SSB opinion, Shari'ah rules on transfer/early settlement, dissenting opinions, member signatures and issuance date (para 59).

An audit and governance committee (AGC) of at least three members is required where the issuer lacks a suitable audit committee, the issuance has high investment risk or material size, and the issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended (paras 62-63).

Shari'ah non-compliance risk is managed by the SCD, which integrates it with operator-wide risk management, identifies/assesses/monitors exposures and mitigating measures, and submits periodic reports to management, those charged with governance and the AGC (para 79).

External Shari'ah audits, where required (high-risk/material/ongoing or open-ended issuances), must be performed at a minimum annual frequency, with the draft report first submitted to the SSB before finalisation (paras 97-98, 103).
Takaful coverage or a mutual Takaful/mutual guarantee model is recommended for high-risk, relatively material investments to address collective fund-provider risk (para 39).

Termination of an ICF issuance requires SSB approval (and regulator/court approval where applicable) and must not result in an unjustifiable material loss to fund providers unless termination is inevitable (paras 104-105).

Restructuring or rescheduling may occur only as a result of the issuer's default/potential default or the issuer's acquisition/merger/corporate restructuring, and requires SSB, fund-provider (via trustee) and, where required, regulator approval (paras 106, 109).
At maturity and liquidation, the SSB supervises the process from a Shari'ah perspective and issues a final SSB report based on financial reporting and external/Shari'ah audit reports (paras 112-113).

The prospectus must be a live, periodically updated document for open-ended issuances and must, at minimum, cover issuer/underlying-operations details, profit/loss-sharing mechanisms and ratios, risks and mitigation, legal framework, transferability/early settlement conditions, and termination/restructuring/default scenarios (paras 118-119).
The operator must retain transaction records for the period set by the respective regulator, or a minimum of seven years in the absence of such a regulatory requirement (para 125).

Financial reports of ongoing and/or open-ended ICF issuances must be prepared at least annually (preferably more frequently), following AAOIFI FAS guidance, with accounting policies approved by the SSB (paras 127-129).
Under Appendix B, the operator must conduct periodic money-laundering risk assessments no later than every 24 months, alongside sanctions-list monitoring and CFT controls (para B2).

KYC and fund providers' due diligence (Appendix B) requires background checks, source-of-wealth and inheritance verification for higher-risk cases, and documentation of any deviation from the standard due-diligence approach (paras B4-B6).
This standard is effective on ICF issuances, on a prospective basis, for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023, with earlier application encouraged (para 140).
divergence_notes: The Fatwa document must record "reservations and dissenting opinion(s), if any, along with the reason(s) for such reservations or dissent" and the names/signatures of dissenting SSB members (para 59f).
"Certain members were of the view that the standard shall only be applicable to commercial ICF issuances because social ICF issuances may need some relaxation on the requirements" (para BC7).

On the collective Takaful/mutual guarantee mechanism: "Certain members were of the view that this should be optional and shall be driven by the local regulations rather than being part of the standard", while others considered it important to safeguard stakeholders (paras BC25-BC26).

On replacing the trustee with an automated portal: "Certain members supported the idea but the majority were of the view that... the appointment of the trustee as a third party is of utmost importance to safeguard the interests of the fund providers" (para BC23).

Guidance on awarding-of-mandate and transaction-close phases applies mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with AAOIFI GS 12 “Sukuk Governance” (para 6).
"Hybrid syndicated financing arrangement" defined as a syndicated financing arrangement including a fully segregated Shari’ah compliant tranche as well as a conventional financing tranche (para 7e).

"Inter-financier agreement" defined as an agreement among financiers/syndication participants describing their respective rights and obligations re the transaction, customer, underlying assets and securities, payment apportionment, etc.; footnote clarifies that in a hybrid arrangement it must be separately prepared and signed for the Shari’ah compliant tranche and the conventional tranche (para 7g, fn 2).
Five key pillars of institutional governance applicable to syndicated financing transactions: Shari’ah compliance, accountability, fairness, transparency, responsibility (para 8 a-e).

Seven governance principles tabulated: (1) Effective Shari’ah compliance structures, (2) Fair treatment of, and amongst, stakeholders, (3) Equitable and fair treatment of, and amongst, syndication participants, (4) Transparent interaction of, and amongst, syndication participants, (5) Effective oversight, (6) Transparency and mutual disclosures, (7) Code of conduct and ethics (para 9).
Under Principle 1, a syndicated financing transaction shall, at a minimum, comply with the requirements of SS 24 “Syndicated Financing” and any other applicable Shari’ah standards (para 9).
Six typical parties to a syndicated financing transaction: lead arranger, arrangers, security agent, facility agent (where applicable), syndication participants, and the customer (para 10 a-f).

Hybrid syndicated financing arrangement permitted only if the overall purpose (including use of underlying assets/proceeds) is Shari’ah compliant and either: (a) the customer's financing needs cannot be met by IFIs alone, and the customer alone (without IFI involvement) approaches CFI(s); or (b) the customer has no Shari’ah preference and has already mandated a CFI arranger, with IFIs willing to join via a separate Shari’ah compliant tranche subject to paras 21, 23(e), 26 and 27 (para 20 a-b).

In a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement: the sanctity of the Shari’ah compliant tranche must be maintained at all times; its arranger(s) must be limited to IFIs; the mandate for that tranche must be awarded specifically among IFIs only; and an IFI involved shall not, in any way, lead, arrange or facilitate (including as agent) the conventional financing tranche (para 21 a-d).

Information memorandum must, in the case of a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, clearly describe the segregation of the Shari’ah compliant tranche from the conventional financing tranche (para 23e).

Lead arranger shall prepare an inter-financier agreement in consultation with all potential syndication participants (para 24); it must at minimum cover 13 items including transaction/security details, rights and responsibilities of parties, early settlement/maturity provisions, pre-exit conditions, transfer of shares, and dispute resolution amongst participants (para 25 a-m).

In a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, two distinct inter-financier agreements shall be separately prepared and signed by the syndication participants — one for the Shari’ah compliant financing tranche and one for the conventional financing tranche; the Shari’ah compliant tranche's agreement must clearly identify and segregate that tranche and name its lead arranger(s), who are responsible for ensuring compliance with the standard (para 26).

The inter-financier agreement for the Shari’ah compliant tranche in a hybrid arrangement must ensure proper enforceability of Shari’ah principles and rules and the tranche's contractual terms, and must specify the Shari’ah-compliant mechanism applicable on default for realisation/liquidation of the respective security or underlying assets (para 27).

BC16: the “Shari’ah Committee of the Shari’ah Board for Review of Accounting and Governance Standards” observed an element of cooperation between IFIs and CFIs for interest-bearing transactions where IFIs sign the same inter-financier agreement in a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement (BC16).

BC17: the Shari’ah Committee advised that in a hybrid arrangement the inter-financier agreement should be prepared separately and signed by the syndication participants for the Shari’ah compliant financing tranche and the conventional financing tranche respectively (BC17).

BC18: the board agreed with the Shari’ah Committee's view (to avoid malpractices in the sector) and amended the standard so that IFIs are not allowed to sign the same inter-financier agreement in case of a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement (BC18).

BC19: the respective central Shari’ah board (CSB) of the jurisdiction, or the SSB of an IFI, may make a case-by-case exception to the separate-agreement requirement on grounds of necessity (e.g. legal enforceability), but the board concluded it is not appropriate to provide such an exception as an option within the standard itself (BC19).

Early exit (pre-exit) by a syndication participant before maturity must comply with the terms of the inter-financier agreement and relevant Shari’ah principles and rules, particularly those related to sale and settlement of debt where a debt is involved (para 45).

Restructuring or rescheduling of a syndicated financing transaction requires thorough review and approval by the respective SSBs of the syndication participants, the customer, and, where applicable, the regulator, to ensure Shari’ah compliance and safeguard parties' interests (para 49).

Change of Fatwa: where a syndication participant's SSB decides to change its Fatwa on the transaction, it must follow the requirements of AAOIFI SS 29 “Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework” and the respective AAOIFI GS on Shari’ah Decision-Making Process, promptly inform other participants and the customer, and collaborate to find a Shari’ah compliant solution (para 42, fn 7, fn 8).
Effective date: this standard shall be effective on syndicated financing transactions executed on or after 1 July 2024; earlier application is encouraged (para 52).

Standard approved unanimously by AAOIFI Governance and Ethics Board (AGEB) at its 31st meeting held 1-2 Muharram 1445H, corresponding to 19-20 July 2023, and finally issued 15 Jumada II 1445H, corresponding to 28 December 2023 (Appendix A; H8).
divergence_notes: BC19 notes jurisdictional/institutional divergence is tolerated on a case-by-case basis: "the respective central Shari’ah board (CSB) of the respective jurisdiction or the SSB of an IFI may make an exception on this matter on a case to case basis on grounds of necessity" (BC19).
BC9 notes that SSB responsibility-sharing and Shari’ah-audit approaches are not uniform, being shaped by "the currently prevalent regulatory frameworks in different countries" (BC9).

standards.title: AAOIFI Governance Standard (GS) 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
linked_standards: AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals
standards.applicability: Applies to Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) along with Islamic social finance institutions such as Waqf, Zakah and Qard-based microfinance institutions, collectively referred to as "the institutions" (para 2); no exclusions stated.
term_names: AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR3); Introduction: Overview (IN1-IN2), Rationale(s) for this standard (IN3), Acknowledgement (IN4-IN5); Objectives of the standard (para 1); Scope (paras 2-3); Definitions (para 4); Part A: Principles of the institutional framework (para 5, principles a-f); Part B: Components of the institutional framework (para 6, components a-g); Proportional application and outsourcing (paras 7-8); Effective date (para 9); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard (Board/working group/executive team lists); Appendix B: A model institutional framework for the implementation of ethics — operative part (para 7, fn 10; BC15), organised by Principle 1: Commitment to ethics at all levels (B1-B6); Principle 2: Formalisation of ethics requirements and expectations (B7-B14); Principle 3: Sustained allocation of resources (human and financial) for ethics (B15-B27); Principle 4: Supporting internal stakeholders to understand, own and practice ethics while encouraging external stakeholders to do the same (B28-B32); Principle 5: Nurturing an organisational culture which encourages and incentivises ethical conduct and discourages and penalises unethical behaviour (B33-B38); Principle 6: Periodic improvement of the institutional framework (B39-B42); Appendix C: Basis for conclusions (BC1-BC16); Appendix D: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H8).
key_points: Standard mandates the adoption of the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals (issued 26 December 2019) and provides an implementation mechanism for it (PR2; IN3c).

Applies to Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) together with Islamic social finance institutions such as Waqf, Zakah and Qard-based microfinance institutions, collectively "the institutions" (para 2).
Standard mandates the adoption of the respective AAOIFI code of ethics and recommends compliance with the relevant AAOIFI governance standards (para 3).

"Institutional framework" defined as the governance and control mechanisms an institution develops/implements to integrate ethics into the routine functions and behaviours of its internal stakeholders (para 4a).

"Internal stakeholders" defined to include the board of directors, Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB), senior management (particularly the CEO), management and staff, plus outsourced third parties including Takaful agents, BancaTakaful agents and call centre agents (para 4b; fn 6).

Institution shall develop its institutional framework based on at least 6 principles: commitment to ethics at all levels; formalisation of ethics requirements and expectations; sustained allocation of human and financial resources for ethics; supporting internal stakeholders to understand, own and practice ethics while encouraging external stakeholders; nurturing an organisational culture that encourages/incentivises ethical conduct and discourages/penalises unethical behaviour; periodic improvement of the institutional framework (para 5a-f).

Institution shall develop an institutional framework comprising at least 7 components: code of ethics; board ethics committee; ethics risk assessment; ethics capacity building programme; self-declaration; ethics incentive and disciplinary mechanism; ethics violation reporting mechanism (para 6a-g).

Institution shall adopt the respective AAOIFI code of ethics and may add additional ethical requirements not inconsistent with it, with supplementary implementation guidelines if necessary (para 6a; B8).
Board ethics committee may be a dedicated committee or an existing committee (such as the governance, risk, audit, or audit and governance committee) assigned the function (para 6b).

Ethics risk assessment shall be conducted periodically to evaluate effectiveness/impact of the institutional framework, followed by a comprehensive improvement plan addressing identified shortcomings (para 6c; B13-B14).

Self-declaration component requires relevant internal stakeholders to periodically self-declare compliance with the respective AAOIFI code of ethics and other applicable organisational policies and procedures (para 6e; B32).

Ethics incentive and disciplinary mechanism must integrate ethical-conduct evaluation into the performance appraisal system (affecting compensation, promotion, benefits) plus a disciplinary mechanism scaled to breach severity, with zero-tolerance for material violations (para 6f; B34-B35).
Ethics violation reporting mechanism requires an anonymous ethics hotline free of retaliation fear, with a timely response/action mechanism while maintaining confidentiality (para 6g; B36-B37).

Outsourcing of institutional framework components requires board ethics committee approval, only after due diligence on third-party risks including integrity, privacy, confidentiality and security (para 8).
Effective date: standard shall be effective on or after 1 July 2024, with earlier application encouraged (para 9).
Appendix B is expressly designated an operative part of the standard providing guidance on the paragraph 6 component requirements (para 7, fn 10; confirmed at BC15).

Board ethics committee's minimum responsibilities include handling ethics-violation claims against members of those charged with governance/SSB/senior management, managing self-declarations of governance members, authorising the CEO to establish a management ethics committee, deciding on a full-time vs part-time ethics officer, approving the institutional framework, and periodically reviewing its effectiveness (B17a-i).

Management ethics committee, where established, shall comprise at minimum a chairman appointed by the board ethics committee, senior management heads (finance, human resources, Shari'ah compliance, operations), an ethics officer serving as secretary, and at least one middle-management employee (B18a-d).
Institution should preferably include at least one female professional in both the board ethics committee and the management ethics committee, respectively (B20).
Ethics positions to be created include ethics officer and ethics champions; institution may appoint a full-time ethics officer or assign the role part-time to an existing employee (B21-B24).
Ethics training shall be conducted periodically, at least annually, for all internal stakeholders, with specific focus on employees dealing with customers and other external stakeholders (B29).

"Ihsaan" defined as the concept of striving for excellence in ethics, achieved when something is done in a manner which, given resources, constraints and circumstances, cannot be done better (fn 18, citing para 10(e) of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics).

Comprehensive institutional-framework review required periodically, covering compliance with the standard including Appendix B, under strict confidentiality; review report with a comprehensive improvement plan to be shared with the board ethics committee (B40-B41).
Institution is encouraged (not mandated) to publish an annual report on implementation of the AAOIFI code of ethics, optionally accompanied by an independent assurance report (B39b; B42).

standards.title: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments (AAOIFI Governance Standard (GS) 17)
linked_standards: AAOIFI GS 10 "Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for Islamic Financial Institutions"
AAOIFI GS 16 "Institutional Framework for the implementation of Ethics"
AAOIFI FAS 34 "Financial Reporting for the Sukuk-holders"
AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals
standards.applicability: Applies to Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating engagements conducted by independent rating agencies on Sukuk and other Islamic finance instruments (para 2), covering Sukuk issued by IFIs/corporates/governments, investment management instruments incl. restricted investment accounts (RIA), unrestricted investment accounts (URIA) or similar offered by non-IFI entities or by IFIs not rated (or rated below target) under GS 10, and other liability/quasi-equity/asset products offered publicly (para 4); highly recommended (not mandatory) for all publicly offered instruments EXCLUDING those offered by IFIs already rated under GS 10 'Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for Islamic Financial Institutions' (para 6); rating agency performing the engagement must itself be a licensed/recognised credit rating agency or Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary (SCF) rating agency meeting GS 10 and this standard's requirements (para 8).
term_names: iAAAs / iAAs / iAs / iBBs / iBs / iCs (rating scale)
standards.structure: Preface (PR1-PR2); Introduction: Overview, Rationale for issuing this standard (IN1-IN6); Objectives of the standard (para 1); Scope (paras 2-4); Responsibility (paras 5-6); Definitions (para 7); Key compliance requirements applicable to rating agencies: Eligibility to conduct ratings (paras 8-9), Ethical requirements (para 10); Assessment scope and benchmarked parameters: Assessment scope for a rating engagement (para 11), Types of instruments - Equity/quasi-equity without guarantee (paras 14-17), Quasi-equity with guarantee (paras 18-20), Liability type (paras 21-22), Asset type (para 23); Establishing benchmarked parameters (paras 24-27): Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules (paras 28-29), Shari'ah governance framework (paras 30-31), Corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance (paras 32-36), Transparency and disclosure (para 37), Ethics and values (paras 38-39), Fiduciary performance and capacity (paras 40-44); Tiered and jurisdiction-specific rating considerations (paras 45-46); Relative weight of benchmarked parameters incl. weightage table (paras 47-48); Limitations of scope and suitability of benchmarked parameters (paras 49-52); Rating scale incl. iAAAs-iCs table (paras 53-56); Principal procedures (para 57); Documentation, archiving and confidentiality (para 58); Reporting (para 59); Effective date (para 60); Appendix A: Adoption of the standard - Board members, Reservation, Working group; Appendix D: Basis of conclusions (BC1-BC27); Appendix E: Brief history of the preparation of the standard (H1-H7).
key_points: Standard applies to Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating engagements conducted by independent rating agencies to provide stakeholders an independent, comparable, assessment-based rating on Sukuk and other Islamic finance instruments' Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities (para 2).

Instruments in scope: Sukuk issued by IFIs, corporate entities or governments; investment management instruments incl. restricted investment accounts (RIA) not registered as separate legal entities; unrestricted investment accounts (URIA) offered by non-IFI entities or by IFIs unrated/below-target under GS 10; and other liability, quasi-equity or asset products offered publicly (para 4).
This standard is a continuation of AAOIFI GS 10 'Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for Islamic Financial Institutions' (PR2).

It is highly recommended (not mandatory) that all publicly offered Sukuk and Islamic finance instruments, excluding those of IFIs already rated under GS 10, obtain a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating, preferably updated annually and announced publicly (para 6).

Eligible rating agency: a licensed/recognised credit rating agency or a dedicated Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary (SCF) rating agency, each having developed capacity/methodology per GS 10 and this standard (para 8).

Eligibility further requires meeting the ethical requirements (para 10), GS 10 paras 11-13 quality control requirements, GS 10 paras 14-17 engagement-acceptance requirements, and GS 10 Appendix B fit-and-proper criteria (para 9).
Ethical requirement: rating agency shall comply with the AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals and other codes insofar as consistent with it (para 10).

Rating combines two aspects: (a) Shari'ah compliance and governance - compliance with Shari'ah principles/rules, Shari'ah governance framework, corporate governance practices, transparency and disclosure, ethics and values; and (b) fiduciary performance and capacity - asset quality/returns and creditworthiness of the originator (para 11).

Instruments are classified into four types for scope/rating-scale purposes: (a) equity/quasi-equity type without guarantee or purchase undertaking; (b) quasi-equity type with guarantee or purchase undertaking; (c) liability type; and (d) asset type (para 13).

Equity/quasi-equity without guarantee: represents residual interest in underlying asset(s), perpetual/convertible, originator has unconditional right to avoid delivering cash/asset, subordinate to all liability and quasi-equity instruments except share capital (para 14); no guarantee or purchase undertaking exists to guarantee capital or return (para 16).

Quasi-equity with guarantee/purchase undertaking: recourse in default is first to the originator (not the underlying asset), risk and reward partially absorbed by originator, giving these instruments substantial liability characteristics (paras 18-19).

Liability type instruments (Murabaha, commodity Murabaha/Tawarruq, Salam, Istisna, and qualifying hybrid Sukuk) are so classified if the liability component (at par value) is more than 50% of total underlying assets and/or the liability component's return is more than 66.67% of the instrument's overall return (para 21(a)-(b)).

Explanation to para 21: this 50%/66.67% classification test is solely for applying this standard's scope requirements and is not a statement of the instrument's Shari'ah compliance, cross-referencing AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard (SS) 59 'Sale of Debt' paras 8/2/2 and 8/2/3 (para 21 explanation, fn 5).

Asset-type instrument: a financing/investment product offered to customers via any acceptable Islamic finance mode, by IFIs unrated (or below target rating) under GS 10, or by other entities publicly offering such products e.g. deferred payment sale or Ijarah based (para 23).

Six benchmarked-parameter aspects are assessed across all four instrument types, with relative relevance varying by type: compliance with Shari'ah principles/rules, Shari'ah governance framework, corporate governance practices, transparency and disclosure, ethics and values, and fiduciary performance and capacity (paras 24-25).
Preferred practice is two separate scores/ratings: (i) Shari'ah compliance and governance (items a-e of para 24) and (ii) fiduciary responsibilities and capacity (item f) (para 27).

Suggested weightage table (para 48): Shari'ah compliance with principles/rules 30-35% across all instrument types; Shari'ah governance framework 15-20% (equity/quasi-equity without guarantee), 10-15% (quasi-equity with guarantee, liability), 5-10% (asset); corporate governance practices 10-15% (5-10% for liability); transparency and disclosure 10-15% (5-10% for liability); ethics and values 10-15% (equity/quasi-equity without guarantee), 5-10% (others); asset quality/returns 25-30% (equity/quasi-equity without guarantee), 15-20% (quasi-equity with guarantee), N/A (liability, asset); creditworthiness of the originator 15-20% (quasi-equity with guarantee), 35-45% (liability), N/A (equity/quasi-equity without guarantee, asset) (para 48 table).
Rating scale is suggested to span 5-10 stepped grades, with a failure in a significant category (particularly compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules) treated as an overall failure (para 53).

Suggested combined rating scale (para 54 table): iAAAs 90%+ (excellent compliance); iAAs 80-89% (very good); iAs 70-79% (good); iBBs 60-69% (highly satisfactory); iBs 50-59% (reasonable, some controversial elements, approved by relevant Shari'ah authorities); iCs below 50% (unsatisfactory, structure considered controversial by several international jurists or noteworthy Shari'ah non-compliance elements present).

For liability-type and quasi-equity-with-guarantee instruments the fiduciary performance element of the rating scale is reduced or eliminated (captured instead via credit ratings); for asset-side instruments the fiduciary element may be eliminated entirely given its irrelevance (para 55).
Fiduciary performance and capacity is the primary rating aspect for liability-type instruments and carries significantly higher weight for quasi-equity-with-guarantee instruments (para 40).

Jurisdiction-specific ratings may amend the hierarchy of benchmarked-parameter resources per local regulation; the agency must document and publicly announce the amended hierarchy, distinguish the rating via a jurisdiction-specific three-letter suffix, and not claim general alignment with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards (para 46(a)-(c)).

Principal procedures, documentation/archiving/confidentiality, and reporting requirements follow GS 10 'Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for Islamic Financial Institutions' paras 37-54 (procedures and documentation) and paras 61-62 (reporting), as suitably amended for this standard (paras 57-59).
Effective date: this standard applies to Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings of Sukuk and other Islamic finance instruments issued on or after 1 July 2023 (para 60).
divergence_notes: iBs-grade instruments: underlying structure 'may not be universally considered compliant but is approved by the relevant Shari'ah authorities' (para 54, iBs row).

iCs-grade instruments: underlying structure 'is considered controversial by several international jurists or there is noteworthy presence of basic elements of Shari'ah non-compliance' (para 54, iCs row).

Public hearing comment noted the standard's instrument classification differs from AAOIFI FASs' classification; board concluded the quasi-equity split (with/without guarantee) is a further sub-classification, not a divergence from the FASs (paras BC24-BC27).

key_points: Objective is to establish a comprehensive framework for consistent and effective application of Shari'ah governance principles to Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates of conventional financial institutions (para 1).
Standard applies to all Islamic finance subsidiaries and Islamic finance associates of conventional financial institutions (para 2).
'Conventional parent' is defined as a conventional financial institution that controls, or exercises significant influence on, an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate respectively (para 3a).
'Islamic finance associate' is an independent IFI subject to significant influence of a conventional financial institution in its governance and managerial decision-making (para 3b).
'Islamic finance subsidiary' is an independent IFI controlled by a conventional financial institution in its governance and managerial decision-making (para 3c).

'Public interest institutions' include listed institutions, institutions with publicly traded securities (e.g. Sukuk), and retail IFIs with investment accountholders/unitholders/participants exceeding 10,000, unless differently defined by the respective regulator (para 3f).
TCWG (Those charged with governance) are the person(s)/organisation(s) responsible for overseeing strategic direction and accountability of the entity, per the IESBA definition (para 3i).

The standard applies irrespective of the conventional parent's ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority), so long as control/significant influence over governance and decision-making exists (para 5).
Shari'ah governance framework must comprise: (a) an SSB, (b) Shari'ah compliance function, (c) internal Shari'ah audit function, and (d) external Shari'ah audit (para 6).

External Shari'ah audit is mandatory for Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates that are public interest institutions after a period of three years from the standard's effective date; strongly recommended for all others and during that period (para 7).
Subsidiaries/associates are subject to the requirements of relevant AAOIFI Standards (including the AAOIFI GSs on Shari'ah governance) as full-fledged IFIs, in addition to this standard (para 8).
Responsibilities, fit-and-proper criteria and other aspects of each governance framework component are the same as prescribed in the relevant AAOIFI GSs (para 9).
An Islamic finance subsidiary/associate must be and act as an independent IFI without undue interference or control/influence from the conventional parent's management (para 11).

TCWG of the subsidiary/associate bears entire fiduciary responsibility to its stakeholders (shareholders and IAHs); this cannot be transferred or delegated to the conventional parent's TCWG merely due to ownership (para 13).
The conventional parent may influence decision-making only at a strategic level, through board membership and board committees, represented in line with its shareholding percentage (para 14).

Conventional parent representatives on TCWG must abstain from voting on issues benefiting the parent at the cost of the subsidiary's/associate's stakeholders, or creating reputational risk for the industry (para 15).

Conventional parent cannot appoint executive management heading/significantly involved in business functions to the subsidiary's/associate's TCWG; heads of independent functions (compliance, internal audit, risk management) and non-executive TCWG members may be appointed, subject to regulatory requirements and GS 1 (2024) paras 36-46 (para 16).

A conventional parent may have dotted-line reporting of key business functions with an Islamic finance subsidiary (but not an associate), giving parent function heads access to relevant information without authority to control/influence managerial decision-making, subject to both boards' approval and regulatory requirements (para 17).

Shared services arrangements between parent and subsidiary/associate must be on an arm's-length basis, approved by both TCWGs and the SSB of the subsidiary/associate, with the parent's TCWG abstaining from the subsidiary's/associate's vote (para 20).

No employee of the subsidiary/associate can be coerced to work for the conventional parent, and the subsidiary/associate cannot lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the parent (para 21).

An Islamic finance subsidiary/associate may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract, but cannot place funds with its conventional parent or any other conventional financial institution, directly or through a third party (para 23).

Financial statements must include adequate, duly segregated disclosures of related-party transactions/balances with the conventional parent per relevant AAOIFI FASs, identifying the nature of contracts under paras 20-23 (para 24).
The standard is effective on or after 1 January 2026, with earlier application encouraged (para 25).

standards.applicability: Applies to the audit of financial statements of a financial institution which conducts business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles (para 1); governs the auditor's objective and responsibilities in forming and expressing an opinion on such financial statements (paras 2-3); no exclusions stated.

key_points: Purpose of this ASIFI is to establish standards and provide guidance on the objective and general principles governing an audit of financial statements of a financial institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles (para 1).

Objective of an audit is to enable the auditor to express an opinion on whether financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, and relevant national accounting standards and practices (para 2).
The phrase used to express the auditor's opinion is "give a true and fair view" (para 2).
The auditor's opinion enhances credibility of financial statements but is not an assurance as to future viability of the institution or the efficiency/effectiveness of management (para 3).

Auditor should comply with the "Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants" issued by AAOIFI and the International Federation of Accountants, to the extent these do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles (para 4).

Ethical principles governing the auditor's professional responsibilities: (a) righteousness, (b) integrity, (c) trustworthiness, (d) fairness, (e) honesty, (f) independence, (g) objectivity, (h) professional competence, (i) due care, (j) confidentiality, (k) professional behaviour, (l) technical standards (para 4).

Auditor should conduct an audit in accordance with ASIFIs, which are auditing standards approved by AAOIFI containing basic principles and essential procedures with related explanatory guidance (para 5).

Auditor should plan and perform the audit with professional competence and due care, recognizing circumstances may exist causing financial statements to be materially misstated, and should expect to find evidence supporting management representations rather than assuming they are correct (para 6).
"Scope of an audit" refers to the audit procedures deemed necessary by the auditor in the circumstances to achieve the audit's objective (para 7).

Audit procedures under ASIFIs are determined having regard to Islamic Rules and Principles, ASIFIs, relevant professional bodies, legislation and regulations that do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles, and, where appropriate, terms of the audit engagement and reporting requirements (para 7).
International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) apply to matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs, provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles (para 7).

An audit is designed to provide reasonable assurance that financial statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement; reasonable assurance relates to the accumulation of audit evidence and to the whole audit process (para 8).

Reasonable assurance also means the auditor has satisfied himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the financial institution's Shari'a Board (para 9).

Inherent limitations affecting the auditor's ability to detect material misstatement: (a) use of sampling while testing transactions and balances, (b) inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system (e.g. possibility of collusion), (c) most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive (para 10).

The auditor's work to form an opinion is based on judgement regarding: (a) gathering of audit evidence, e.g. deciding nature, timing and extent of audit procedures, and (b) drawing conclusions from audit evidence gathered, e.g. assessing reasonableness of management's estimates (para 11).

Other limitations may affect persuasiveness of audit evidence available for conclusions on aspects of the financial statements (e.g. related-party transactions); certain ASIFIs identify specified procedures that may provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence absent (a) unusual circumstances increasing risk of material misstatement beyond normal expectation, or (b) any indication that material misstatement exists (para 12).
Auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements (para 13).

Responsibility for preparing and presenting financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation/regulations rests with management of the financial institution, with regard to be given to the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations (para 13).
The audit of the financial statements does not relieve management of the financial institution of its responsibility for those statements (para 13).
This Standard is effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H., corresponding to 1 January 1998 A.D. (para 14).
The Standard of Objective and Principles of Auditing was adopted by the Board in its meeting No. (11), held 2-3 Muharram 1417 A.H., corresponding to 19-20 May 1996 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).

standards.title: Auditing Standard No. (2): Auditor's Report
linked_standards: Financial Accounting Standard No. (1): General Presentation and Disclosure in the Financial Statements of Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions
standards.applicability: Applies to the form and content of the independent auditor's report issued on financial statements of a financial institution that conducts business in conformity with Shari'a Principles; guidance may also be adapted for auditor's reports on financial information other than financial statements (para 1). No exclusions stated.
term_names: Auditing Standards for Islamic Financial Institutions (ASIFI)
standards.structure: Introduction (paras 1-4); Basic Elements of the Auditor's Report (paras 5-26) covering Title (6), Addressee (7), Opening/introductory paragraph (8-11), Scope paragraph (12-16), Opinion paragraph (17-22), Date of report (23-24), Auditor's address (25), Auditor's signature (26); Auditor's Report - illustrative unqualified report (paras 27-28); Modified Reports (para 29); Matters That Do Not Affect the Auditor's Opinion - emphasis of matter (paras 30-35); Matters That Do Affect the Auditor's Opinion - qualified/disclaimer/adverse (paras 36-40); Circumstances That May Result in Other Than an Unqualified Opinion - Limitation on Scope (41-44) and Disagreement with management (45-46); Effective Date (para 47); Adoption of the Standard (unnumbered).
key_points: Purpose: establish standards and guidance on the form and content of the auditor's report for audits of financial statements of Islamic financial institutions conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Principles (para 1).
Auditor's report must contain a clear written expression of opinion on the financial statements taken as a whole (para 4).

Ten basic elements of the auditor's report: title, addressee, opening/introductory paragraph, scope paragraph, reference to ASIFIs and relevant national standards, description of work performed, opinion paragraph, date of report, auditor's address, auditor's signature (para 5).

Opening paragraph states the financial statements and the institution's undertaking to operate per Shari'a Rules and Principles are management's responsibility; the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion based on the audit (para 9).

Scope paragraph states the audit was conducted per ASIFIs and relevant national standards/practices that do not contravene Shari'a Rules and Principles, planned and performed to obtain reasonable assurance the financial statements are free of material misstatement (paras 12-13).

Audit is described as including: test-basis examination of evidence, assessing accounting principles used, assessing significant management estimates, and evaluating overall financial statement presentation (para 14).

Opinion paragraph states whether financial statements give a 'true and fair view' in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Supervisory Board and the financial reporting framework (paras 17-18).

Financial reporting framework is determined by the AAOIFI, statutory requirements, rules of professional bodies, and the development of general practice within a country, with consideration of the institution's undertaking to conform to Shari'a Rules and Principles (para 19).
Opinion may additionally address compliance with other statutory or legal requirements specified by relevant statutes or law (para 20).

When financial statements are distributed extensively outside the country of origin, it is recommended the auditor refer to the accounting standards of the country of origin (e.g., AAOIFI) in the report (para 22).
Auditor should date the report as of the audit completion date, and should not date it earlier than the date the financial statements are signed or approved by management (paras 23-24).
Report should name a specific location, ordinarily the city where the auditor maintains the office responsible for the audit (para 25).
Report should be signed in the name of the audit firm, the personal name of the auditor, or both, as appropriate (para 26).

Unqualified opinion is expressed when financial statements give a true and fair view under the identified financial reporting framework, implicitly confirming proper determination and disclosure of accounting principle changes (para 27).

Modified reports fall into two categories: (1) matters that do not affect the opinion (emphasis of matter), and (2) matters that do affect the opinion (qualified opinion, disclaimer of opinion, or adverse opinion) (para 29).

An emphasis of matter paragraph is mandatory for a material going concern problem, and should be considered for other significant uncertainties whose resolution depends on future events (paras 31-32).
In extreme cases involving multiple significant uncertainties, the auditor may consider it appropriate to express a disclaimer of opinion instead of adding an emphasis of matter paragraph (para 34).

An unqualified opinion may not be possible where there is (a) a limitation on the scope of the auditor's work, or (b) a disagreement with management on Shari'a Rules/Principles implementation, accounting policy acceptability/application, or disclosure adequacy (para 36).

A qualified opinion is expressed as being 'except for' the effects of the matter, when the effect of a scope limitation or disagreement is not so material and pervasive as to require an adverse opinion or disclaimer (para 37).

A disclaimer of opinion is expressed when a scope limitation's possible effect is so material and pervasive that the auditor has not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence (para 38).

An adverse opinion is expressed when a disagreement's effect is so material and pervasive that a qualification would not adequately disclose the misleading or incomplete nature of the financial statements (para 39).
Any opinion other than unqualified requires a clear description of substantive reasons and, unless impracticable, a quantification of the possible effects on the financial statements (para 40).
Illustrative disagreement example uses straight-line depreciation at annual rates of 5% for buildings and 20% for equipment as the basis for a qualified-opinion adjustment (para 46).

Standard effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H. / 1 January 1998 A.D. (para 47); adopted by the Board at meeting No. (11), held 2-3 Muharram 1417 A.H., corresponding to 19-20 May 1996 A.D. (Adoption of the Standard).
